experiences.title: Accenture Interview Experience | PADA Role (On Campus )
experiences.full_content:
I recently went through the Accenture campus placement process and was thrilled to be selected! The process was structured into three stages: an online test, a communication assessment, and a technical + HR interview. Here’s a detailed breakdown of my experience:

Application Process

I applied for the position through my college's campus placements. The selection process was straightforward and well-organized, consisting of the following stages:

1. Online Test

The online test included two sections: Aptitude and Coding.

Aptitude Section:

The questions were fairly easy, and I prepared for this section using YouTube videos, which provided helpful insights into concepts and question patterns.

Coding Section:

The coding section had two problems:

Floyd’s Triangle: A straightforward problem that I solved with ease.
Matrix Problem (Minimum Distance): This task involved calculating the minimum space required to move from one position to the middle of the matrix. It was moderately challenging but manageable with logical thinking.
Overall, I found one question easy and the other moderately difficult, and I successfully solved both.

2. Communication Round

This stage was a speech test designed to assess communication skills. It evaluated:

Pronunciation
Grammar
Fluency
Clarity
The focus was on ensuring effective and professional communication.

3. Technical + HR Interview

The final stage combined technical questions and an HR discussion, primarily based on my resume and projects.

Technical Questions:

They asked detailed questions about my e-commerce project, specifically about the authentication mechanisms I implemented.
I was also asked about the technical and non-technical skills I gained from the project.

General HR Questions:

"Where do you see yourself in five years?"
"Why do you want to join Accenture?"

Opportunity to Ask Questions:

At the end of the interview, I was encouraged to ask questions. I took this opportunity to inquire about the role's expectations and the company's culture, which gave me valuable insights.

Key Takeaways

Difficulty Level:

Aptitude: Easy
Coding: Easy to Moderate
Overall Process: Balanced and straightforward

Preparation Tips:

Aptitude: Use YouTube videos to understand concepts and solve practice questions.
Coding: Practice problems involving logic-based solutions and basic algorithms.
Communication: Focus on clarity and fluency to excel in the speech test.

Final Verdict

Selected!

The recruitment process was a rewarding experience, and I’m excited to start my journey with Accenture!

experiences.title: Accenture Interview Experience | Role: Advanced application engineering analyst | Campus visit: 2024
experiences.full_content:
In July, Accenture commenced the registration process for the Advanced Engineer Hiring (AEH) program at VIT. A pre-placement talk was held on August 27, followed by the assessment test on September 11.

Assessment Overview

The assessment consisted of two parts: a cognitive round and a coding round. Only candidates who performed well in the cognitive assessment were eligible to proceed to the coding round. In the coding round, candidates were shortlisted based on the complete execution of their programs within half the allotted time. The coding questions were of easy to medium difficulty.

Communication Assessment

A week after the coding test, we received a link for the communication assessment. I recommend watching a tutorial on YouTube to prepare for this part. After completing the communication test, I received an interview link four days later.

Interview Process

The interview primarily focused on my resume and basic HR questions. Out of thousands of applicants, 156 were selected, and I was fortunate to be one of them.

Topics Covered

Cognitive Test Topics:

Flow charts
Verbal reasoning
Sentence arrangement
Antonyms and synonyms
Basic quantitative aptitude (directions, symbols in patterns, choosing the best conclusion)
Paragraph-based questions
Data analysis from graphs and pie charts

Odd one out
Set theory
Human relations
Passive and active voice
Articles (fill in the blanks)

experiences.title: Accenture Interview Experience | Summer Internship | Oct 2024 [Shortlisted]
experiences.full_content:
Hi everyone,
I am excited to share that I was recently selected for Accenture's summer internship program for 2024. I hope that by detailing my interview experience, I can assist those preparing for similar opportunities. The selection process consisted of four stages, which I will break down below.

1. Aptitude and Cognitive Test

Duration: 90 minutes
Format: 90 multiple-choice questions (MCQs)
Topics Covered:English ability (grammar, comprehension)
Critical thinking
Abstract reasoning
Basic MS Office skills
Network security

Tip: Time management is crucial. Regular practice with aptitude questions, especially those related to reasoning and verbal ability, will be beneficial.

2. Coding Round

Duration: 45-60 minutes
Questions: 2 questions of easy to medium difficulty (similar to LeetCode)
Topics: Arrays, strings, dynamic programming, and basic data structures
Tip: Focus on problem-solving patterns, particularly from platforms like LeetCode. The problems were manageable, but understanding optimal solutions can save valuable time.

3. Communication Assessment

This round assessed my listening and speaking skills through an automated system, where I listened to audio clips and responded accordingly.
Tip: Practice speaking clearly and concisely. Engaging in listening exercises and mock interviews can greatly enhance your performance in this round.

4. Final Interview

Format: Technical + HR
Focus Areas:Discussion of my projects (I highlighted my text summarizer and other web-based projects)
General HR questions (strengths, weaknesses, etc.)

Tip: Be well-prepared to discuss your projects in detail, including the tech stack, challenges faced, and improvements made. For HR questions, honesty and confidence are key.

Conclusion

Overall, my experience was smooth, and preparation on platforms like LeetCode and GeeksforGeeks (GFG) proved invaluable. I hope this breakdown provides insight into the interview process for Accenture’s summer internship program. Good luck to everyone preparing for their own opportunities!

experiences.title: Accenture   Interview Experience | System Engineer Associate | 2024
experiences.full_content:
I recently applied off-campus for the position of System Engineer Associate at Accenture. After successfully clearing all the assessment rounds, I was invited to the Virtual Interview Round, scheduled for August 23, 2024, at 11:30 AM. I joined the interview lobby at 11 AM and waited for nearly an hour before the interview commenced at 12:07 PM.

The interviewer began by introducing himself and then asked me to introduce myself. The conversation flowed into discussions about my achievements, projects, internship experience, skills, and the workshop I organized at my university. He also inquired about my least favorite subjects and how I managed to overcome the challenges associated with them. Additionally, there were some questions related to SQL.

Overall, the experience was positive, with the questions primarily focused on my resume and the projects I had worked on.

Key Points to Remember:

Timely Arrival:

Join the interview lobby early (you joined at 11 AM for an 11:30 AM interview).
Be prepared for potential delays (your interview started at 12:07 PM).
Self-Introduction:

Have a concise and impactful self-introduction ready, highlighting your background, education, and key experiences.
Resume Focus:

Be prepared to discuss every detail in your resume, especially your achievements, projects, internship experience, and skills.
Emphasize any leadership or organizational roles, such as the workshop you organized at your university.
Handling Challenging Subjects:

Be ready to talk about your least favorite subjects and how you overcame challenges related to them. This shows problem-solving skills and resilience.
Technical Questions:

Brush up on key technical skills mentioned in your resume (e.g., SQL in my case) since questions may focus on these areas.
Positive Attitude:

Maintain a positive attitude throughout the interview, even when discussing challenges or areas of improvement.
Be Prepared for a Resume-Centric Interview:

Expect questions to revolve mainly around your resume and projects rather than general or hypothetical scenario

experiences.title: Accenture Interview Experience Software Developer
experiences.full_content:
Interviewing for a software developer role at Accenture typically involves a comprehensive process designed to evaluate both technical skills and cultural fit. Here’s a detailed breakdown of what you can expect:

Application and Screening

Resume Submission: Apply through Accenture’s career portal or a job board. Ensure your resume highlights relevant technical skills, projects, and experience.
Initial Screening: A recruiter or HR representative will review your resume to see if you meet the basic qualifications for the role.

Phone or Video Screening

Recruiter Call: This initial call usually focuses on your background, motivation for applying, and understanding of the role. You might be asked about your experience with specific technologies or projects.
Technical Screening: You may have a technical phone interview with a recruiter or a junior technical team member. This could include basic coding questions or technical problem-solving scenarios.

Online Assessments

Coding Tests: Expect to complete one or more online coding assessments. These tests often involve solving algorithmic problems, data structure questions, or simple coding challenges.
Technical Aptitude: Some assessments may test your understanding of key programming concepts, system design, or problem-solving abilities.

Technical Interviews

Technical Phone or Video Interview: This is usually conducted by a senior developer or a technical lead. You might be asked to solve coding problems live, discuss your approach to problem-solving, or explain your past projects.
Coding Questions: Prepare to write code on the spot, solve algorithmic problems, or debug code. Familiarize yourself with common coding problems and their solutions.
System Design: You may be asked to design a system or architecture, discussing trade-offs, scalability, and performance considerations.

Behavioral Interviews

Behavioral Questions: These assess your soft skills and how you work within a team. Be prepared to discuss past experiences using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Topics might include teamwork, leadership, conflict resolution, and time management.
Cultural Fit: Accenture places emphasis on alignment with its values and culture. Be ready to discuss how you fit with the company’s core values and work environment.

Case Study or Practical Task

Technical Case Study: In some cases, you may be given a practical task or case study relevant to the role. This might involve working on a coding challenge, analyzing a system, or solving a real-world problem.
Project Discussion: Be prepared to discuss your previous projects in detail, including your role, the technologies used, and the impact of the project.

Panel Interviews

Interviews with Multiple Team Members: You may meet with several team members or managers to assess how well you fit with the team and company culture. Each interviewer may focus on different aspects of your skills and experience.

Offer and Negotiation

Job Offer: If successful, you will receive a formal job offer outlining salary, benefits, and other terms.
Negotiation: You may have the opportunity to negotiate aspects of your offer, such as salary, start date, and work location.

Feedback and Follow-Up

Feedback: While feedback is not always provided, some candidates may receive insights into their performance.
Follow-Up: The recruitment team will keep you informed about next steps, including any additional documentation or requirements.

Preparation Tips:

Practice Coding: Use platforms like LeetCode, HackerRank, or CodeSignal to practice coding problems and algorithms.
Study System Design: Review key concepts in system design and architecture.
Review Past Projects: Be ready to discuss your past work in detail, including the technologies you used and the problems you solved.
Understand Accenture’s Culture: Research Accenture’s values and recent initiatives to align your answers with their culture.
Prepare Questions: Have thoughtful questions ready about the team, role, and company.
Overall, the interview process for a software developer role at Accenture is thorough, combining technical assessments with behavioral evaluations to find candidates who are both technically proficient and a good fit for the company’s culture

experiences.full_content:
Candidate Information

Status: B.Tech student of Electronics & Instrumentation Engineering 2025 Pass out Batch
Location: Kolkata, West Bengal, India
Interview Date: 4th September, 2024
My name is Avrajeet Ghosh and I’m a student of Electronics and Instrumentation engineering dept from Narula Institute of Technology.

It was an Accenture On-Campus Drive for 2025 pass-out B.Tech candidates.

They offered us 2 Roles -

Associate Software Engineer (ASE)
Advanced Associate Software Engineer (AASE).
They conducted an online Pre-placement talk in the month of July 2024.

Recruitment Process

Cognitive & Technical Assessment
Coding Assessment
Communication Round
Technical + HR Round

Round 1: Cognitive & Technical Assessment

Section 1: Aptitude

This round is the initial round of their recruitment process. The time given for this round was 90 minutes. The difficulty of this round was easy-moderate.

90 questions were given consisting of a total of 6 sections:  English Ability, Abstract Reasoning, Critical Reasoning, Pseudo Code (Loops, Operators, Recursions), MS Office & Common Application, and Computer Networking Security & Cloud (Situation-Based Questions).

A moderate level of practice would be enough to clear this round.

After completing the assessment, the results were given whether you proceed or not. The message would be given through WhatsApp and Mail within 5 mins.

Section 2: Coding Assessment

2 coding questions were given. 45 minutes were given to complete this round. The questions were -

Rebound Height
Count the highest decrement of temperature in an array (Sub Array)
After completing the assessment, the results were given whether you proceed or not. The message would be given through WhatsApp and Mail instantly.

Note: Both Cognitive and coding assessments happened on the same day. For me, it was on 26th August 2024. Both the rounds were conducted online but we were instructed to take that from the College campus only. The instructions were given by Accenture officials. A PAN card is mandatory to sit for the Accenture campus drive.

Section 3: Communication Assessment

This segment evaluates communication proficiency utilizing specialized software, encompassing both listening and speaking. To ensure accuracy, please maintain a quiet environment and ensure a robust internet connection and try to attempt this round at midnight. Throughout this phase, your communication skills are assessed through various tasks:

Reading aloud provided texts.
Listening to a narrative and accurately repeating it within a specified timeframe.
Responding to inquiries presented.
Just a Minute
In my experience, while the communication tasks were manageable, the software's sensitivity was remarkably high. Even minimal background noise, such as my breathing, was detected as external sound, creating some challenges in maintaining seamless communication.

After completing this round, you would receive a message through WhatsApp and mail saying that you've completed this round.

Note: A good quality headphone is required to take this round. No Bluetooth headphones are allowed, use a wired headphone with noise cancellation microphone. I would suggest taking the test at midnight because external noises are captured and their software is very sensitive. If they sense minor sounds, you would not be able to take the test.

Before the interviews, you would be getting mail regarding slot booking of your interview. You must select a preferable slot according to your needs and book the slot as soon as possible.

Round 2: Technical + HR Interview

Though it seems to be a Technical + HR round for me it was not purely technical round and my interview was 25 mins on 4th September, 2024.

In the Interview round, questions were -

Introduce yourself.
What is your hobby?
Are you pass out graduate or pursuing final year?
Your final year project?
How you implement that system (For me it’s a Hybrid Project)?
What are the technologies you used?
In future what do you want to implement in your project?
Which language you used for your project?
Is it your solo project or group project?
What is your role in your project?
When you feel proudest in your life and why?
Same as when you feel lowest in your life and why?
If you are the team leader and 1 of your team members cannot able to complete his/her task then what should you do?
If your project is not completed within time then what should you do?
If there is a conflict between your team members then how you manage that situation?
If your project is not completed yet but the day is near to submit your project then what should you do?
The interviewer was very satisfied with my statements and confident. Further, she asked me if I had any questions for her. I asked her a few questions related to the training period after onboarding.

After waiting for nearly about 1 month I got the mail of selection for the ASE role on 28th September, 2024 and on the same day, I received a letter of intent.

Company: ACI Worldwide

Role: Associate Software Developer

Date: 09/08/2024

I recently interviewed with ACI Worldwide for the position of ASE. The interview process consisted of three rounds: Technical, Managerial, and HR. Here's a detailed breakdown of my experience.

Round 1: Technical Round

Question: Introduce yourself.

Approach: I provided a brief introduction, covering my educational background, key projects, and relevant skills.

experiences.title: ACI Worldwide Interview Experience | Associate Software Engineer | Full time (On-Campus)
experiences.full_content:
The interview process with ACI Worldwide took place on campus, specifically at the Pune Institute of Computer Technology (PICT). For the 2019-2023 batch, ACI Worldwide was hiring for both Developer and DevOps roles. The process was structured into five distinct rounds, starting with an online assessment (OA) and followed by a series of offline interviews held at the ACI office in Pune.

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an Online Assessment consisting of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and code snippets, primarily in Java. The test covered a range of topics including Java, Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs), Operating Systems (OS), Database Management Systems (DBMS), and Cloud-based concepts. The level of difficulty was moderate, but the key challenge was to complete the test quickly. Candidates were required to write code snippets on paper, so practicing coding without an IDE was crucial.

Round 2 & 3: Technical Interviews

The second and third rounds were technical interviews at the ACI office. The focus was primarily on the candidate’s resume, with a strong emphasis on data structures and algorithms (DSA). Questions included implementing algorithms such as Merge Sort and Quick Sort (using the first or last element as the pivot). Another task was to write code to delete the middle node from a linked list. Other questions that some candidates faced included Breadth-First Search (BFS), matrix operations, basic tree problems, and graph-related questions.

PS: We had to write code on paper.

The questions focused on the projects listed on the resume. For instance, questions asked were: why this project, the tech stack used, and reasons behind those choices. I asked myself A specific question: why did you choose MongoDB over SQL and create a schema if you want to use SQL for your project?

PS: A deep understanding of the projects was crucial for this round.

Round 4: Managerial Round

The fourth round was a managerial interview, which was less technical and more focused on understanding the candidate’s familiarity with ACI Worldwide’s work environment. Questions covered topics such as the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), Agile methodologies, and some basic DSA problems like swapping two numbers without extra space. This round was designed to gauge the candidate’s fit within the company’s operational framework rather than their technical skills.

Round 5: HR Round

The final round was an HR interview aimed at assessing how candidates handle pressure and specific situations. This round was more about evaluating personality and behavioral traits rather than technical knowledge. There were no definitive right or wrong answers; instead, the focus was on how well candidates managed stress and responded to various situational questions.

Overall Experience:

The interview process was comprehensive and challenging, with each round testing different aspects of a candidate's skills and fit for the role. From coding on paper to in-depth project discussions and pressure handling in HR, the experience was designed to thoroughly evaluate both technical prowess and interpersonal qualities. Candidates who prepared well on coding without an IDE, had a strong understanding of their projects, and were familiar with the company’s methodologies likely had a better chance of success.

experiences.title: Adobe Interview Experience | Product Intern | On Campus 2024
experiences.full_content:
When it comes to interviews, every step counts, from the initial online assessment to the final round. I recently went through this process, and I'm excited to share my experience with you. I hope it provides insights and helps you prepare better for your own interviews.

Online Assessment

The first stage was an online assessment consisting of two coding problems and 30 MCQs covering C, DBMS, and OOPS. The coding problems ranged from easy-medium to medium-hard difficulty. I managed to get fully accepted solutions in the last 5 minutes, even though I only had partial solutions after 50 minutes of coding. The MCQs were a mixed bag for me—I had little idea about some of the questions and had to make educated guesses.

Pro Tip: If you encounter a tricky C programming question, remember that you can check its output using the compiler provided for the coding problems. This trick saved me precious time and helped me cross-check my answers.

Interview

There was only one interview round, which began with a discussion about my projects. The interviewer asked if I had deployed one of my projects. I had, but unfortunately, it didn't open for 5 minutes due to technical issues. This could have thrown me off, but the interviewer was kind enough to tell me to relax. This taught me a valuable lesson—don't get tense when things don’t go your way.

We then moved on to coding problems. The interviewer shared a CodePair link, complete with inbuilt test cases, similar to the online assessment. The first question was to merge two sorted arrays. I explained both possible approaches.

Next came a problem about finding the minimum swaps needed to make a set of parentheses balanced. My initial solution passed only 3 out of 15 test cases. Feeling the pressure, I dry-ran my code on an example. The interviewer explained the issue, and after rethinking my approach, I managed to pass 12 out of 15 test cases.

The third problem involved making a queue from stacks. This time, the interviewer asked me to explain my approach without writing the code. I used comments to explain my O(n) to amortized O(1) solution, and the interviewer seemed satisfied.

With some time left, the interviewer asked one more question: how to find the middle of a linked list. I quickly described two different approaches, and the discussion wrapped up smoothly.

Toward the end of the interview, I asked the interviewer about his role and the projects interns typically work on. I also requested feedback with a smile, and he mentioned that I seemed enthusiastic about showing my projects, which he found positive.

The next day, I received a call informing me that I had been selected.

Takeaways for Aspiring Candidates

Stay Calm Under Pressure: Technical issues can happen to anyone, but it’s important to stay composed and focused on the task at hand.
Be Thorough with Your Projects: If you’ve worked hard on your projects, be enthusiastic about sharing them. It leaves a good impression.
Ask for Feedback: Engaging with the interviewer and asking for feedback shows that you are keen on improving yourself.
Keep Learning: Even if your initial solution doesn't work, don't get discouraged. Take the feedback, rethink your approach, and give it another shot.
I hope this article helps you in your preparation and gives you the confidence to tackle your next interview. Good luck!

experiences.title: Airtel Interview Experience for MIS Analyst
experiences.full_content:
Recently, I had the opportunity to interview at Airtel Bharti for an MIS role. While I ultimately didn’t succeed in the final business meet, the experience itself was incredibly enriching and taught me valuable lessons.

The interview process consisted of three rounds: two technical rounds followed by a business meet. I successfully cleared the technical rounds, but unfortunately, I struggled during the business round.

In the business round, one of the key questions asked was:
"What data points would you require for cross-selling analysis?"

Although gathering such data is a part of my current job routine, I found myself overwhelmed during the interview. I got tangled in a web of words and was unable to articulate my thoughts effectively. After the meeting ended, I was left reflecting deeply on my response, grappling with the "play of thoughts" that haunted those moments.

Determined to improve, I decided to work on enhancing my logical and critical thinking skills. Below, I’m sharing some strategies that have helped me strengthen my thought process, which I believe can also benefit others preparing for similar business meets or interview scenarios.

8 Steps to Strengthen Logical Thinking and Problem-Solving Skills

Practice Puzzles and Games
Engage in activities like Sudoku, chess, or logic puzzles. These games challenge you to think strategically and enhance problem-solving capabilities.
Study Logic and Critical Thinking
Explore books and online courses on logic and critical thinking. These resources offer structured methods to approach problems and arguments effectively.
Read Analytically
When reading articles or books, practice breaking down arguments by identifying premises, conclusions, and evaluating the evidence provided.
Ask Questions
Cultivate curiosity by frequently asking “Why?” and “How?”. This practice helps you uncover the root causes of issues and develop deeper insights.
Solve Real-World Problems
Apply logical and analytical thinking to everyday challenges. This could involve analyzing data, creating budgets, or planning and executing projects.
Practice Programming Logic
Learning to code is an excellent way to boost logical thinking. It teaches you to think sequentially and solve complex problems methodically.
Reflect on Your Thinking Process
After solving a problem, take time to reflect on your approach. Consider what strategies worked well and identify areas for improvement.
Engage in Debates and Discussions
Participate in debates and discussions to train yourself to think quickly and defend your viewpoints logically.

Conclusion

The failure in my Airtel interview turned out to be a valuable learning experience. It made me realize the importance of a strong, structured thought process, especially when tackling business problems. I hope the steps I’ve shared here will help others facing similar challenges in interviews or professional settings.

The assessment duration was 90 minutes, which allowed ample time to complete most questions. I managed to finish in 30 minutes and used the remaining time to review my answers. Results were released two days later, with 18 candidates shortlisted, including myself.

Round 2: Technical Interview

The technical interview began with a brief introduction, followed by questions about my projects: Music Recommendation App, QR-Code Generator, and Weather Application.

Music Recommendation App: The interviewer asked about the project’s purpose, tech stack, and backend design, which I developed independently. We discussed scalability, specifically on automating song additions to the database, and recommendations, for which I suggested using APIs (like Spotify) for dynamic trends. I also proposed implementing a machine learning algorithm for recommendations, explaining my decision to use a database due to limited AI/ML experience.
QR-Code Generator: This project, utilizing NPM packages to convert URLs into QR codes, was straightforward, and we discussed its implementation briefly.
Subject Knowledge: I was asked about my current subjects—Computer Networks, Operating Systems, and Data Science. Questions included RAM’s function, SQL basics (primary keys, joins), and a terminal task to display system information using Linux commands. Additionally, I debugged and explained a Python file, fixing syntax and indentation errors, which showcased my troubleshooting skills.
The interviewer, Puneet Sharma, was very supportive, creating a comfortable environment to discuss these projects and technical tasks.

Round 3: Managerial Interview

After 48 hours, I was invited to the managerial interview, conducted by James Park, a senior manager with extensive experience at Akamai. He began by sharing his career experiences, emphasizing the importance of group projects.

Teamwork & Projects: We discussed my involvement in university communities and the Music Recommendation App as a team project, where I explained my backend contributions. He appreciated the relevance of my coursework, including Computer Networks and Operating Systems, particularly the networking fundamentals crucial for Akamai’s field.
Learning Experience: I asked about the internship’s scope and his experiences at Akamai. He shared how interns' work remains impactful and ongoing within the company. His candid insights into Akamai’s culture made this round insightful.

Round 4: HR Interview

This brief, 10-minute interview began with an informal conversation about my hometown, Jammu. The HR representative shared her experiences visiting Jammu, creating a relaxed atmosphere. We discussed challenges faced by startups in Bangalore and factors that contribute to their long-term success. I also inquired about the internship’s project scope, remote setup, and potential for full-time conversion.

Three candidates, including myself, were selected for the internship. This experience was incredibly rewarding, especially with the supportive and insightful interactions throughout each round.

experiences.full_content:
I recently went through the recruitment process for a 6-month SDE Intern position at Amazon, and though I didn’t receive an offer, the experience was highly insightful. Here’s a detailed account of my journey to help you prepare for a similar opportunity.

Application Process

The process started on 21st July 2023 when I received an email titled:

"Amazon invites you to apply for a 6-month Amazon Internship."

The email outlined the following steps:

Step 1: Fill out the Hiring Interest Form via the provided link.
Step 2: Watch for the next steps email scheduled for 24th July 2023.
I promptly completed the form and awaited further communication.

Online Assessment Details

On 24th July 2023, I received an email outlining the details of an Online Assessment (OA) scheduled for 26th July 2023.

Assessment Structure:

RoleCompetenciesTimeSDE 1 InternCoding Assessment70 minutesWorkstyles Assessment15 minutesFeedback Survey5 minutes

Instructions:

Read guidelines on dos, don’ts, and technical troubleshooting.
Fill out the application form (estimated 30 minutes, no time limit).
Receive the OA link immediately after submitting the form.
Complete the OA within the given 90-minute time frame.
I ensured I was well-prepared and completed the assessment in the allotted time.

Clearing the Online Assessment

On 29th July 2023, I received an email congratulating me on clearing the Online Assessment. The email also detailed the next step:

A single interview round scheduled for 9th August 2023.
Links to preparation materials were provided to assist in getting ready for the interview.

Interview Details

Key Interview Information:

Mode: Online (meeting invite to follow).
Duration: 45-60 minutes.
Competencies:Coding (Data Structures and Algorithms).
Coding (Problem Solving).

Preferred Language: Any programming language (Java preferred).

Interview Experience

The interview took place on 9th August 2023 and comprised three parts:

1. Introduce Yourself

I gave a brief overview of my education, interests, and aspirations.

2. Project Discussion

The interviewer asked me to discuss the projects listed in my resume. I explained:

Mental Health Prediction App
Chat Application
Music Web App
I highlighted the technologies used, challenges faced, and my contributions to each project.

3. Coding Question

The interviewer presented the following problem:
Problem: In a given sorted array, find the index of a specified element.

Approach:

I used binary search and explained the logic, edge cases, and time complexity during implementation.

Outcome

On 11th August 2023, I received an email stating that I was not selected for the role. Although the outcome was disappointing, the process provided invaluable learning experiences.

Key Learnings

Time Management: Completing assessments within strict timelines requires practice.
Project Explanation: Be ready to clearly explain your projects, emphasizing their impact and your role.
DSA Mastery: Concepts like binary search and foundational algorithms are essential—master them thoroughly.
Resilience: Rejections are part of the journey. Treat each experience as a learning opportunity.

Conclusion

While I didn’t secure the internship, this process taught me essential lessons and motivated me to improve further. For anyone preparing for an Amazon internship, I recommend:

Practicing coding regularly.
Strengthening problem-solving skills.
Staying confident and focused throughout the process.

During my 3rd year, I had the opportunity to interview with Amazon for a 6-month internship. The interview was both challenging and insightful, offering a valuable learning experience.

experiences.title: Amazon  Interview Experience|  6 months SDE
experiences.full_content:
Hey everyone! This blog post outlines my interview experience with Amazon, highlighting the challenges I faced, the questions I encountered, and the valuable lessons I learned.

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

I received an email from Amazon WOW (Off-Campus) to fill out an interest form for an SDE (6-month) intern position. Subsequently, I was provided with a job link on Amazon Careers to apply for the role. After submitting my application through the portal, I received a link for the Online Assessment (OA).

The OA round consisted of two coding questions—one easy and one medium-level data structure and algorithm problem. I successfully solved both questions, passing all test cases well within the time limit. Following this technical assessment, there was a workstyle evaluation that included behavioral and HR questions to assess my personality and work style.

After completing the OA, I received confirmation that I had qualified for the interview round.

Round 2: Interview

The interview was conducted via Amazon Chime. The interviewer explained the expectations — if I was able to solve the first question, he would then ask a second one; otherwise, he would ask follow-up questions based on the first problem.

We started with the first coding question. The problem was: Given an array of integers where each element occurred exactly k times, except for one element which occurred less than k times. You need to identify that element. The array was sorted. This was a slight variation of this LeetCode problem 540. Initially, I provided a brute force solution using maps. The interviewer then prompted me to solve the problem using a counter variable. After that, he asked me about the time complexity of the solution and requested further optimization. I suggested solving the problem using Binary Search since the array was sorted. Initially, I struggled to arrive at the correct solution, and the interviewer gave me a few hints. Despite this, I couldn't complete the code successfully.

Then, the interviewer asked follow-up questions. The first was about the time complexity of inserting elements into a map, to which I responded, "O(1)." He then asked, If we have a map of size 4 and are adding elements one by one, how do we maintain constant time complexity when the map reaches size 4? Explain why the time complexity is still O(1).

Unfortunately, I was not offered the SDE intern position at Amazon, but it was a valuable learning experience nonetheless.

experiences.title: Amazon Interview Experience for  SDE-2
experiences.full_content:
Preparation Timeline

March 2023 - May 2023:
Practiced random problems and participated in LeetCode contests to build momentum. Earned a Knight status on LeetCode.
June 2023 - October 2023:
Focused on DS Algo problems on LeetCode, solving approximately 300 medium and 50 hard questions. Also practiced topic-wise questions to cover most areas.

Interview Process

Online Assessment (OA):

I applied through the careers portal and received an OA test link within 2 days.
The OA had 2 problems: one medium and one hard. Solved the first problem completely and passed 10/15 test cases for the second one.
The test also included a lot of Leadership Principles (LP) and design choice scenario-based questions.
A week later, the recruiter informed me I had cleared the OA and discussed my experience and upcoming rounds. Took two weeks to prepare for LLD and System Design Interviews.

Interview Rounds

Round 1 - DS Algo + Leadership Principles (LP):

After a brief 10-minute introduction, I was asked a backtracking question which I managed to solve and run successfully.
The interviewer grilled me on LP questions, but I had real-life examples, which helped me answer fluently.
Next, I was given a tree-based question with some modifications. Though it was a standard problem, the modifications made it hard, and I couldn't solve it without hints.
Round 2 - Concurrency + LP:

This round was a mix of Low-Level Design (LLD) and coding, with one string-related problem requiring a concurrency approach optimization.
I implemented the code and dry-ran it with an example, which impressed the interviewer. I also answered LP questions well.
Round 3 - LP + High-Level Design (HLD):

This round was mentally exhausting, with the first 30 minutes focused on granular LP questions.
Despite the grilling, I had real-life examples to support most of my answers.
After LP, I was asked a system design question. Unfortunately, I was too anxious and exhausted to answer it properly. The interviewer’s lack of communication didn’t help, and I struggled to perform my best.
Round 4 - Bar Raiser:

The round started immediately with no introduction. The interviewer gave me an LLD question, and I provided a design that satisfied the functional requirements.
I discussed trade-offs, synchronization, mutexes, and included them in my design.
After 45 minutes, the focus shifted to LP questions, which I answered well, and the round ended 5 minutes early with smiles.

Outcome

After the Bar Raiser round, I was confident and even celebrated with a pizza. However, four days later, the recruiter informed me that I didn’t meet the bar raiser’s expectations, and they wouldn’t be making an offer. I was shocked and felt extremely disappointed.

Final Thoughts

Sometimes, despite hard work and preparation, success may not come your way due to circumstances beyond your control. If things don’t work out, my advice is to accept the situation, move on, and find peace within yourself. Don’t compare your journey with others or be too harsh on yourself.

Wishing everyone the best of luck in their journeys!

experiences.title: Amazon Interview Experience for SDE Intern | 6 Month intern
experiences.full_content:
In August 2024, I interviewed for the Software Development Engineer (SDE) 6-month Intern position at Amazon. The interview process was thorough and consisted of three main rounds. It was off campus and took me 1 month for the whole process.

First Round

July end, The first round was a coding challenge that included multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and a coding problem. The MCQs covered topics like Computer Networks (CN), Operating Systems (OS), Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs), and Linux. Each section had five questions, including some related to coding outputs.

For the coding problem, I had to calculate the number of Binary Search Trees (BSTs) that can be formed with `n` nodes. This problem is addressed in detail [here](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/construct-all-possible-bsts-for-keys-1-to-n/).

Second Round

Aug 10 - In the second round, I participated in a coding assessment on HackerRank, which was not proctored. The assessment featured two medium-level array problems. The focus was on array manipulation and algorithmic efficiency.

Final Round

Aug 29 - The final round was a virtual interview lasting about an hour, with two interviewers (though only one asked questions). It began with a brief introduction. Only 2 DSA questions were asked. The technical questions included:

1. An array problem -- where I had to find the minimum number of swaps required to group all females in a circular table, an array of characters 'm' and 'f', using the sliding window method.

example :
F  F M M F
min swaps=0

F F M F M F M
min swaps =1
F F F F M M M

Count the Number of Females: First, find out how many 'f' characters there are in the array. Let's call this number total_count.

Sliding Window Technique:

Start with a window of size total_count and count how many 'f' characters are in this window.

Calculate the number of swaps needed by subtracting the number of 'f' characters in the window from total_count.

Move the Window:

Slide the window one step to the right. Update the count of 'f' characters by adding the new character that enters the window and removing the old character that leaves the window.

Track the minimum number of swaps needed.

Handle the Circular Array.

2. A problem involving finding the maximum sum in a binary tree where no two adjacent nodes (parent and child) are considered. The solution to this problem involves dynamic programming and is explained in detail [here](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/maximum-sum-nodes-binary-tree-no-two-adjacent/).

During the interview, I was advised to clearly communicate my thought process and discuss my approach before starting to code. It’s important to consider time and space complexities and aim to complete the questions within the allotted time. As i was not able to complete the 2nd question on time , which put me at disadvantage. Interviewer suggested me to frequently give mock interviews and practice more coding questions on a timer.

Verdict : Not Selected.

experiences.full_content:
Amazon came to our campus.

ROUND 1- Online Assessment

There were two questions 1st was easy and 2nd was medium level.

ROUND 2-Interview

Amazon takes only one interview for SDE INTERN

Interviewer asked me to introduce myself and then told me to describe any project.

We are given a matrix(MXN) which is sorted row-wise and column-wise .Given a target element return the pair {row,col} is target exist in the matrix , else return {-1,-1}.

I gave three approaches for this

1st) Traverse the whole matrix and if we found that element then return respective row and column number else return {-1,-1}

T.C=O(MXN)

S.C=O(1)

2nd) Apply binary search on each row

T.C=O(MXlog(N))

S.C=O(1)

3rd) Take a pointer place it at 1st row and last column ,since the matrix is sorted row wise and column wise if( matrix[row][col] targetE row col--;

else if matches then return that particuar row column

T.C=O(M+N)

S.C=O(1)

After giving 1st approach she asked me time and space complexity and asked to optimize them then after giving 2nd approach she asked time and space complexity and  said that you are usking advantage of row wise sorted ,i want you to think of column wise sorted as well

After third approach she first said to dry drun ,like how approach is working and asked time and space complexity and said to code third approach.

After code she asked me to dry run 2 examples and to write time and space complexity of all approaches

Given a BST you have to replace each node's  value with the sum of all node which are greater than it .

Traverse tree in inorder way and store inorder in vector and then traverse tree again (with any traversal) and find the element in inorder vector and take sum of all the elements after it and replace the nodes value with sum and do the same for rest.

T.C=O(N)+O(NN) approx (for inorder traversal+any traversal  traversing vector )

S.C=O(N)(for storing inorder)+O(h)( auxillary stack space h=height of tree)

She said she dont want extra vector space that i was taking and told me to optimize

2nd approach) Apply inorder in opposite manner ,inorder is left root right ,reverse inorder will be right root left in this way we can access largest element first and we dont need to store in vector ,for largest element we have to replace it with zero since none element is greater than it. and we can take sum variable and add nodes value to it then we can replace nodes value with( sum-nodes value)

T.C=O(N) for inorder

S..C=O(h)  where h is height of tree

After writing code she asked me to dry run for 2 test cases

Verdict: I didn't get selected

In November 2022, Amazon conducted a hiring drive at Anna University, Chennai, for the role of Support Engineer. This was their second drive of the year, following the Software Development Engineer (SDE) hiring process in August. Here’s a detailed account of the hiring process and my journey.

Hiring Process Overview

1. Online Test

Format:

2. Technical Interview I

experiences.full_content:
I'm a student from NIT Warangal, where Amazon recently conducted their recruitment drive. They allowed students from CSE, ECE, and EE to participate, with around 350 students eligible for the initial coding round.

Round 1: Online Assessment

Coding:

I don't recall the exact questions since the assessment was held offline in the labs. However, they were the kind of problems you could solve using data structures like deques or vectors, and also using unique elements. One question was related to minimizing inefficiency. Each student received a different set of questions, including problems like k-spikes.

WorkStyle Assessment:

The time limit wasn't clear (though the mail mentioned 20 minutes, there was no timer). It's crucial to approach this section carefully, as it seemed to be a significant factor in the selection process.

From this round, 40 students were shortlisted for the next stage, which took place online the following day.

Round 2: Interview

There was a single interview round for the Summer Internship, lasting between 45 minutes to 1 hour and 20 minutes. The interviewer outlined the process: introductions, two coding questions, followed by discussions on CS subjects and projects.

After introductions, the interviewer posed the first question: finding the rare vowel string. Here’s a related problem: [Group Anagrams and return in lexicographically sorted order](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/problems/print-anagrams-together/1 ).While I tried a pair-sorting  approach with time Complexity of O(nlogn), the interviewer hinted to the key-Encrption technique to solve in O(N), and we discussed this for about 35-40 minutes. We then moved on to the second question .

The second question was about finding the Covid Spread: [Covid Spread](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/problems/covid-spread--141631/1). I discussed solution through DFS(depth-First-Search), but the interviewer requested a BFS(Breadth-First-Search) approach. I explained him the pseudo code and in between I got stuck in thinking of the syntax and optimization. After discussing time and space complexities, I coded my solution. This took almost the entire allotted time, and we concluded the interview after 1 hour and 20 minutes.

The interviewer then asked if I had any questions. I inquired about potential tasks if selected, the prerequisites, and how to improve for future opportunities. The interviewer provided thoughtful responses.

Unfortunately, when the final list was released the next day, I was not among the 13 students selected for the 2-month internship.

Pro tip: Don’t stay silent during the interview. Try to articulate your thoughts out loud. If you're facing any difficulty in solving a question, feel free to ask the interviewer for hints.

experiences.title: Amazon ML Summer School Program  2024 Experience
experiences.full_content:
I’m a final-year BTech student passionate about Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This year, I had the privilege of being part of Amazon ML Summer School 2024, a prestigious program aimed at equipping students with essential ML skills and offering insights into Amazon’s groundbreaking innovations.

In this article, I’ll share my journey, key takeaways, and tips for aspiring participants. Whether you’re an ML enthusiast, a tech lover, or curious about such programs, I hope my experience inspires you!

About Amazon ML Summer School

Amazon ML Summer School is a prestigious program designed to provide in-depth knowledge of ML. Led by Amazon Scientists, the program combines technical expertise with mentorship, fostering innovation among students.

With ML revolutionizing industries, this program equips students with skills to build successful careers in AI and ML. It’s open to second- and third-year students from recognized institutes in India who are passionate about learning from experts.

The Selection Process

Getting into the program starts with an application process where students share their academic background, programming skills, and ML interest. The process includes:

Selection Test:

Conducted in multiple slots, the test assesses foundational knowledge and problem-solving skills. It has two parts:The test lasts 75 minutes, requiring both speed and precision.

Part 1: Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs) covering:

ML Concepts: Supervised/unsupervised learning, algorithms, and applications.

Programming Fundamentals: Python basics, syntax, and logic.

Mathematics for ML: Probability, statistics, and linear algebra.

Part 2: Programming Problems:

Two medium-level data structure and algorithm (DSA) problems. Candidates can use any language, though Python is recommended.

Preparation Tips:

Practice ML and Python-related MCQs on platforms like GeeksforGeeks.

Solve medium-level problems on LeetCode or HackerRank, focusing on arrays, strings, and hash maps.

Virtual Sessions and Mentorship

After clearing the test, I was thrilled to receive my selection email! The program schedule included eight modules covering key ML areas:

Supervised Learning
Unsupervised Learning
Sequential Learning
Deep Neural Networks
Reinforcement Learning
Dimensionality Reduction
Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs)
Causal Inference
The sessions started with basics and progressed to advanced concepts, making them accessible to everyone. Dedicated doubt-clearing sessions allowed mentees to interact with Amazon’s ML scientists, who patiently addressed every question.

The month-long journey was packed with engaging content, practical insights, and mentorship opportunities. The structured learning and interaction with experts made it an unforgettable experience.

Internship Opportunities at Amazon

At the end of the program, mentees had the opportunity to apply for internships in the Data Science domain. Amazon shared an interest form, and the hiring process included an online test, interview rounds, and final selection.

Successful candidates secured a six-month internship to work on cutting-edge projects alongside Amazon’s talented teams.

Concluding Thoughts

The Amazon ML Summer School 2024 was more than just a program—it was a journey of learning, growth, and inspiration. From mastering ML concepts to interacting with Amazon’s scientists, it enriched my skills and fueled my passion for AI.

This program taught me the value of curiosity, perseverance, and collaboration. It reminded me that the possibilities in AI and ML are limitless for those willing to push boundaries and embrace challenges.

Tips for Aspiring Mentees

Build a strong foundation in ML, programming, and math.
Regularly practice coding and solve real-world problems.
Stay curious, ask questions, and leverage mentorship opportunities.
Focus on personal growth and collaboration—both are as crucial as technical skills.
If you’re passionate about AI and ML, I highly recommend applying to this program. It’s a golden opportunity to learn from experts, explore cutting-edge technologies, and connect with like-minded innovators.

Good luck on your journey! Keep learning, stay inspired, and never stop chasing your dreams.

experiences.title: Amazon Offcampus 6 months internship  Experience 2024 | SDE Intern
experiences.full_content:
After registering for the Hack on Amazon Hackathon, my team successfully cleared two rounds. Unfortunately, we were eliminated after that. A few days later, I received an email from Amazon inviting me to apply for a six-month internship.

Aptitude Test On August 21st, I received the OA (Online Assessment) link, which consisted of two coding questions. Each question had 15 test cases, and I managed to solve about 19-20 test cases in total. While the problems were of medium-hard difficulty, I encountered TLE (Time Limit Exceeded) for 2-3 test cases

The OA also included around 60-70 questions based on Amazon's leadership principles. This part is crucial for shortlisting, so it's important to stay calm, answer carefully, and avoid skipping any questions.

A few days later on 24 August I received a mail from Amazon that I was shortlisted for an interview scheduled for September 2nd. I had read that there would only be one interview, lasting an hour, so I prepared thoroughly.

Interview Process I started the interview with a well-prepared introduction, which made a strong impression on the interviewer. The interview consisted of two DSA (Data Structures and Algorithms) questions:

A modified version of the Koko Eating Bananas problem.
Finding the missing number in an array.
For the first problem, I initially started with a brute force approach(Linear Search) before moving to an optimal solution. Since I was solving this problem for the first time, I initially wrote a brute force version of the is Possible function for the binary search, which I later realized and corrected with the optimal approach. I spent around 40-45 minutes on this question. Interviewer seemed satisfied after this and told me to proceed to next question.

The second question, finding the missing number, was fully solved. I explained five different approaches to solving this problem, carefully considering the flaws in each method and improving the algorithm each time. This demonstrated my ability to think through all possible cases, and the interviewer seemed satisfied with both solutions.

Afterward, I asked some questions about Amazon and the interviewed extended for 5 more minutes around 1 hr 5 minutes.

From my experience, I realized that solving the problem perfectly isn't the most important factor for Amazon. What truly matters is your thought process, how you approach the problem, and how well you write and explain your code. Even if you don’t completely solve a problem, it’s essential to demonstrate solid reasoning and consider edge cases.

As Amazon promised to roll out results in 5 business days, Finally on 5th business day after interview, on September 9th, I received the exciting news that I was selected for the six-month internship at Amazon!

TakeawaysFocus on clean, understandable, and modular code: Writing code that is easy to follow and modular is crucial, as it reflects your ability to organize and structure your thoughts effectively.
Solving 100% of the problem isn’t everything: It’s okay if you don’t fully solve the problem, but make sure to clearly convey your thought process and approach.
Think through every edge case: Demonstrating that you’ve considered all possible scenarios, including edge cases, is key to impressing the interviewer.
Patience is necessary: I was told I’d receive the interview link by August 30th, but didn’t get it until September 1st. I had almost lost hope, but suddenly, I was notified on September 1st that my interview was scheduled for September 2nd.
Keep practicing DSA: For MAANG companies, DSA (Data Structures and Algorithms) remains a critical component, so consistent practice is essential.
Always believe you are the best. Be confident and never doubt yourself. Don’t think that MAANG companies are only for extraordinary people. Even those working there once had the same doubts. Believe in your potential and go for it!

experiences.title: Amazon WoW Interview Experience || SDE 6-Months Internship Opportunity
experiences.full_content:
On November 5, 2024, I received a form link from Amazon WoW for a 6-month internship opportunity. After completing the form, I was provided access to a Mettl coding challenge assessment, which needed to be completed within two days.

Round 1: Technical Assessment

This round included:

Questions on Operating Systems, DBMS, Linux, Data Structures, and Algorithms.
A coding problem to solve.
After clearing this round, I received a test link for the second round.

Round 2: Coding and Behavioral Assessment

The second round required candidates to:

1. Fill in their details on the Amazon platform to generate the test link.

2. Complete:

Two coding questions.
Behavioral questions based on Amazon Leadership Principles.
After successfully clearing this round, I received a link for the final interview, scheduled two days later.

Round 3: Final Interview

The final interview was conducted on the Amazon Chime platform on November 18, 2024, from 4:00 to 5:00 PM. Two interviewers were present during the session.

Structure of the Interview

1. Introduction:

The interview began with a request for a brief self-introduction.

2. First DSA Question (String Manipulation):

I explained two approaches to solve the problem.
The interviewers asked me to code the second approach and explain its time and space complexity.

3. Second DSA Question (Design a Data Structure):

The problem was to design a data structure supporting insert, delete, search, and getRandom operations in O(1) time.
I explored various solutions, considering linked lists and arrays, and reasoned through their time and space trade-offs.
My final solution combined an array and a hash map, where the hash map stored array values as keys and their indices as values.
The interviewers asked how I would handle duplicate values in this setup.

4. Debugging Exercise:

To test my debugging skills, they commented out a line of code and asked me to analyze its impact.
I used dry-run examples to identify the issue, which satisfied them.

Outcome

I believe the interview went well, but I have not received a verdict. As of mid-December 2024, the interview process appears to have concluded, but I have not received any communication regarding selection or rejection.

Final Thoughts

The experience was challenging yet rewarding. It provided an excellent opportunity to showcase my technical skills, problem-solving abilities, and adaptability under pressure. While the outcome is uncertain, I remain positive about the learning gained from this process.

I am a 4th-year student at IIT Roorkee, and I recently secured a Data Science role at American Express through the on-campus placement process. Here’s a detailed overview of the placement process, including my test and interview experiences.

About the Role

Positions Offered: Software, Data Science, and Product Development roles (focused on Data Science).
Eligibility: Open to all branches, with no CGPA criteria.
CTC Offered:UG: ₹23.4 LPA
PG: ₹24 LPA

Placement Process

Step 1: Resume-Based Shortlisting

Although resume shortlisting was part of the process, all applicants were allowed to proceed to the online test.

Step 2: Online Test

Platform: Unstop
Sections (MCQ format):Numerical Ability: 24 questions
Logical Reasoning/Data Interpretation: 24 questions
Coding: 12 questions

Difficulty Level: Easy to Medium
Interestingly, 4–5 questions in my test matched questions from a PDF document I had referenced, shared by students from another IIT.
Link: Test Questions Reference

Step 3: Interview Process

The interview consisted of two rounds, blending technical and HR discussions:

Round 1: Technical + HR Interview

Introduction: A brief self-introduction to start the conversation.
Resume Discussion:I was asked to describe all my projects.
During one project discussion, the interviewer asked about my unique contributions. I admitted that the project was more of a learning experience than a significant contribution. The interviewer appreciated my honesty and moved on.

SQL Query: I analyzed two SQL tables and made inferences based on the data provided.
Guesstimate Question: I was asked to estimate how many 1 kg packets of Bikaneri Bhujiya are sold in a year.
Company Knowledge: The interviewer quizzed me about my understanding of American Express.

Round 2: Technical + HR Interview

Two Important Things: The interviewer asked me to share two key points from my resume or life. I mentioned a project and an internship.Follow-up: I explained that these experiences involved solving real-world problems, and I had included them because they were meaningful to me.

Guesstimate Question:The task was to estimate the weight of the International Space Station.

Puzzle Question:The puzzle involved 10 boxes of balls, where one box contained balls weighing 20 gm each, and the rest had balls weighing 10 gm each. The task was to determine the box with 20 gm balls using the minimum number of weighings.

Honesty Matters: Acknowledging gaps in your contributions can leave a positive impression if communicated sincerely.
Structured Problem-Solving: Even if you don’t arrive at the correct solution, demonstrating your thought process can work in your favor.

Securing a Data Science role at American Express was a significant milestone in my academic journey. The process was rigorous but rewarding, testing both my technical and analytical abilities. experiences.title: Ansys Software Pvt. Ltd. Interview Experience || SDE Intership + Performance based PPO
experiences.full_content:
Recently, I underwent an exciting yet challenging interview process with Ansys Software Pvt. Ltd. The journey began with approximately 500 applicants, of which only 50 were shortlisted for the second round. Here’s a detailed breakdown of my experience throughout the various stages:

Round 1: Shortlisting

The first round was purely based on resume screening. Out of the 500 applicants, only 50 were selected to move forward. It was a highly competitive process, making it essential to have a strong resume that highlighted relevant skills.

Round 2: Pen and Paper Test

The second round consisted of a written test featuring five questions, which included a mix of Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) and open-ended problems. Here are the questions I encountered:

Exponential Squaring (Fast Modulo Multiplication)
This question tested our ability to optimize large power calculations under modulo constraints. For more details, you can check out resources on GeeksforGeeks.
Linked List Problem
A standard question requiring solid DSA fundamentals focused on manipulating linked list nodes efficiently.
Mathematical Logic Problem
This problem assessed my problem-solving skills and understanding of mathematical reasoning.
Custom Sorting Question
We were tasked with sorting elements based on custom-defined logic, which tested our ability to design algorithms on the spot.
Carrom and Pot Problem
This was one of the most interesting and complex DSA problems. Given a carrom board with the queen at a fixed position and several other coins, we needed to determine how many safe pots the queen could make without obstruction. This question combined geometry and DSA knowledge.
Following this round, only 9 candidates were shortlisted for the next stage.

Round 3: The Interview (Final Round)

In the final round, I faced my first panel interview with three interviewers, lasting about an hour and 20 minutes. The session began with cross-questions related to the problems from the previous round. The panel aimed to understand my thought process and problem-solving approach, diving deep into the logic I applied during the pen-and-paper test.

The discussion then shifted to frontend and backend development, my area of expertise. Uniquely, they requested to view my GitHub profile, where they selected one of my repositories and began asking questions about it. This included an in-depth review of my code and my approach to solving specific issues. I followed this with backend-related questions, confidently responding based on my experience with Node.js.

This round was a blend of managerial and technical questions, assessing not only my technical expertise but also my ability to handle real-world problems and communicate my solutions effectively.

The Final Result

Out of the 9 candidates interviewed, only 2 were selected, and I was fortunate to be one of them. It was a challenging yet rewarding experience that provided valuable insights into my strengths and areas for improvement.

This journey underscored the importance of being well-prepared across various domains and maintaining a solid grasp of fundamentals. Transitioning from 500 applicants to being one of the two selected was an intense but fulfilling experience.

As a final-year Computer Science Engineering student, I had the opportunity to participate in the on-campus recruitment drive conducted by ANZ. Here’s a structured overview of my interview experience, the questions I faced, and some key takeaways for future aspirants.

Interview Rounds Overview

The recruitment process consisted of three stages:

Gamified Round

This round assessed logical reasoning, problem-solving skills, and cognitive abilities through a gamified format.

Coding Round

Problem 1: A scenario-based question that required a unique application of Dijkstra’s algorithm.
Problem 2: Finding the number of triplets that satisfy a given condition.

Technical + HR Round

A comprehensive evaluation of technical knowledge, problem-solving abilities, and behavioral attributes.

Technical Interview Questions

1. Project Discussion

As my resume highlighted machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) projects, the interviewer explored this domain extensively. Key questions included:

Explain your project and the motivation behind it.
What ML and DL models did you implement?
Write and explain linear regression code for a given dataset.
What are Random Forests and Support Vector Machines (SVMs)? Explain their working principles.
How did you utilize Numpy and Pandas libraries in your project?
How many epochs did you use during training, and why?
Did you work with any known datasets? If so, what were their dimensions?
Describe the data preprocessing techniques you applied.
This part of the interview emphasized my understanding of ML algorithms and my hands-on experience with real-world datasets.

2. Core Algorithms and Data Structures

The interviewer tested my grasp of fundamental algorithms:

Implementation and explanation of Dijkstra’s algorithm.
Discussing real-life applications of Dijkstra’s algorithm.

Behavioral and HR Questions

In addition to technical questions, I was assessed on communication skills, cultural fit, and motivation through questions such as:

Why should we hire you?
What do you know about ANZ?
Describe a challenge you faced in a project and how you overcame it.
What are your career aspirations, and how does this role align with your goals?
General questions on teamwork and problem-solving.

Key Takeaways

Prepare Your Projects Thoroughly: Be ready to discuss every aspect of your projects, including algorithms, implementation details, and reasoning behind your choices.
Master Core ML/DL Concepts: Understand algorithms like linear regression, random forests, and SVMs, along with popular libraries like Numpy and Pandas.
Revise Algorithms and Data Structures: Brush up on fundamental algorithms like Dijkstra’s and their practical applications.
Practice Behavioral Questions: Use the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to structure your answers effectively.
Research the Company: Knowledge about ANZ’s mission, values, and innovations can leave a strong impression.

Conclusion

Interviewing with ANZ was a challenging yet rewarding experience that highlighted the importance of balancing technical depth with effective communication. I am delighted to share that I was selected for the company.

For those preparing for campus placements, focus on project clarity, algorithmic problem-solving, and behavioral interview techniques.

I noticed there were very few articles detailing the Apple interview experience, so I decided to share mine in hopes that it might help others. Here's a breakdown of my journey.

Apple was looking for individuals with strong communication and interpersonal skills who could collaborate effectively across diverse business and technical teams. They sought proactive candidates with a positive attitude toward problem-solving.

Overview of Interview Rounds:

Resume Shortlisting
Online Test
Interview Round 1 - Technical (Eliminatory)
Interview Round 2 - Techno-Managerial

Round 1: Resume Shortlisting

In this round, Apple shortlisted candidates based on their resumes. Only those without backlogs were selected to move forward.

Round 2: Online Test

The online test consisted of a coding question and MCQs.

Coding Question:
(This was a LeetCode problem.)Imagine you're playing a game where you need to cross a sequence of stones to reach the final stone. Each stone has a number indicating the maximum steps you can jump forward. Starting from the first stone, determine whether you can reach the last stone. Return true if it's possible, otherwise false.

Input: [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]
Output: true
Explanation: Jump 1 step from the first stone to the second, and then take 3 steps to jump directly to the last stone.

MCQs:
There were a total of 10 questions focused on core computer science topics such as:DBMS
OS
OOPs
DSA
Tip:
Read and practice a lot of MCQs related to these core subjects online. Coding practice on LeetCode is essential.
Around 50 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 3: Technical Interview (Eliminatory)

Platform: Webex & CoderPad (for pair coding)
This round was conducted online, and the company asked for our preferred time slots. I was interviewed by a Senior Software Engineer, who was very polite and approachable. Here’s what was asked:

Coding Questions:Merge Sort: I was asked to implement Merge Sort, analyze its time complexity, and discuss any edge cases.
Time Complexity Analysis: I was given several code snippets and asked to analyze their time complexity.
SQL Query: A tricky SQL query was presented, and I was asked to provide its output.

Project-Related Questions:A detailed overview of all the projects listed on my resume.
A few management-related questions, such as how I handled conflicts during my projects and my learning methodology.

The interviewer concluded by asking if I had any questions, to which I responded with some template questions.

Tip:
Be very thorough about the projects on your resume. Understand them completely, including any technical details.

Around 35-40 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 4: Techno-Managerial Interview

Platform: Webex & CoderPad (for pair coding)
This round was also conducted online, and I had prepared for a range of managerial questions. However, the interview turned out to be quite different from what I had expected. I was interviewed by a Senior Software Manager who asked me to jump straight into pair coding.

Coding Question (Pair Coding):N-Queens Problem:
The manager described the problem vaguely but didn't directly mention the problem name. I recognized it as the N-Queens problem and was able to write a working solution in 25 minutes.N-Queens Problem

Managerial Questions:How do you manage conflict with your teammates?
What are the challenges you faced in your projects?
How impactful do you think your project is?

Random Questions (Twists!):When was your college built?
Why do you like your college?

Tip:
Your confidence and how well you can manage challenges are key in this round. Stay calm, be honest, and answer confidently.

The Result

Out of all the candidates, 5 were selected for the Software Development Engineer (SDE) intern role, and I was one of them!

Final Thoughts

I hope you find this article helpful in preparing for your Apple interview. Good luck to all future candidates!
Thank you for reading!

I recently appeared for an interview at Argusoft, and here’s how my experience went:

1. Online Test

The process began with an online test that included Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, and Technical MCQs. The technical section primarily focused on Data Structures, Algorithms, C, Java, and SQL. The questions tested fundamental programming concepts like arrays, linked lists, and basic query writing. Time management was key since there were about 40 questions in 60 minutes.

2. Technical Round 1

The first technical interview was conducted over a video call. The interviewer started with basic OOPs concepts, including inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. I was asked to explain real-world examples of these principles. This was followed by a coding problem to find the longest palindromic substring in a given string. I chose to write the solution in Java, and the interviewer asked me to explain my approach, which involved dynamic programming.

Some other questions included:

Explain the difference between Stack and Queue.
What is the time complexity of merge sort?
How do you optimize database queries?
I was also given a simple SQL query to write that involved using joins.

3. Technical Round 2

In the second technical round, the focus shifted to projects mentioned in my resume. The interviewer asked detailed questions about one of my major projects, including the technology stack and the challenges faced. I was also asked to explain the design patterns used, specifically the MVC pattern, which was a core part of my project.

Some additional coding questions were given during this round, such as:

Implement a function to reverse a linked list.
Write a SQL query to find the second highest salary from an Employee table.
I was also asked about unit testing and version control systems, as Argusoft follows an agile development process.

4. HR Round

The final round was an HR interview where I was asked questions related to my long-term goals and why I wanted to join Argusoft. They also discussed the company’s work culture and projects. A few situational questions like how would you handle a tight deadline? were also asked.

experiences.full_content:
Interview Process Overview:

Stages:

Online Test
Technical Interviews: 2 Rounds

Online Test

Many candidates found the online test challenging; however, those familiar with the Striver DSA Sheet found it manageable.

Questions:

Question 1 (Greedy):An easy greedy algorithm problem.

Question 2 (Dynamic Programming):A straightforward 1D DP question for those experienced in dynamic programming.
The task was to find the maximum sum in an array, with options to either move sequentially or jump to prime numbers ending in 3.
This solution involved memoization and establishing proper logic for jumps based on number properties.

Question 3 (Graph):A problem involving a directed cyclic graph.
Initially, I considered using Kahn’s algorithm due to the directed nature, but it turned out to be simpler to solve with a DFS-based approach since the graph was cyclic.
I partially solved the question, achieving 2.5 out of 3 correct solutions, which placed me 5th overall.

Observation: Some candidates were selected despite lower scores, likely influenced by diversity and inclusion considerations.

Interview Rounds

Technical Interview — Round 1

Resume Review: The interviewer had reviewed my resume but did not ask related questions, which is common among higher-paying companies that prioritize skills over resume details in initial rounds.

Questions:

C Language Code with Pointers:I was required to code using C pointers and memory allocation techniques with malloc and calloc.
I requested to use C++ due to my familiarity with its syntax, but I was asked to proceed with C, which negatively impacted my performance.

Memory Allocation:I explained the differences between static, dynamic, and register memory allocation in C/C++.
In a follow-up, we discussed the storage mechanisms for static and constant variables.

Linked List:I was tasked with reversing a linked list in k-sized parts.
I coded it from scratch and presented two approaches, although I encountered some issues.

Copy Mechanisms:I explained the concepts of shallow copy and deep copy.

Feedback: The interviewer indicated that my performance on the first question significantly influenced their assessment.

Verdict

Outcome: Not selected.

Result: Out of the candidates interviewed, five were selected, primarily based on their strong foundational skills.
