experiences.title: Chubb Business Services  Interview Experience  | Trainee Software Engineer | On-campus
experiences.full_content:
Hi everyone! This community has been a tremendous help during my interview preparation, and I’m thrilled to give back by sharing my first-ever interview experience. My journey with Chubb Business Services was full of learning, even though I couldn’t clear the final round. I hope this walkthrough of the process, challenges, and takeaways inspires and supports others preparing for their own journeys.

About the Opportunity

Chubb Business Services visited VIT on 8th August for recruitment across its four campuses (Vellore, Chennai, Bhopal, Amravati), offering the role of Trainee Software Engineer for B.Tech students in CSE and IT branches.

Recruitment Process Timeline:

Pre-Placement Talk and Applications: 10th August onwards
Online Assessment: 16th-17th August
L1 Interviews (Technical): 20th-21st August
L2 Interviews (Managerial/Behavioral): 22nd-23rd August
Virtual Training for Selected Candidates: September-December
Shortlisted candidates for the Online Assessment were announced on 13th August.

Stage 1: HackerRank Online Assessment

The assessment featured five coding problems:

3 Easy-Medium problems
2 Medium-Hard problems

Key Concepts:

Arrays
Greedy Approach
Recursion
Graph Traversal (Minimum Cost Path)
HashMaps
Time Allotted: 2 hours
I managed to solve 4 out of 5 questions, with partial test cases cleared for the fifth. Students solving 2.5–3 questions were shortlisted for the interviews.

Stage 2: L1 Technical Interview

This round focused on technical proficiency based on my introduction and resume.

Interview Details:

Panel: Two interviewers (one asked most questions).
DBMS & OOPs: Explained 4 pillars of OOPs with examples.
Discussed relational vs. non-relational databases from my projects, with examples.

Projects:

Walked through a GitHub repository—cloned and explained the code.
Wrote and explained a GET API for my MERN project.

Certifications:

Discussed my AWS Cloud Practitioner certification, including cloud models, pricing, and scaling techniques.

DSA and Java:

Explained why I prefer Java for DSA, mentioning Garbage Collection and Generics.
At the end, I asked about their training program and team assignments. My queries were answered in detail.

Pro Tips for L1 Interview:

Keep your introduction concise and highlight meaningful experiences.
Know your resume inside out—the interview will revolve around it.
Be ready to explain your projects, certifications, and technology choices.
Shortlisted candidates were announced within two days, and I progressed to the next round.

Stage 3: L2 Managerial/Behavioral Interview

This round had a panel of five members, with one leading the discussion.

Key Questions:

My leadership roles as Content Head and General Secretary in college clubs: What I learned and how I applied those lessons.
Why I consider myself a good fit for Chubb.
How my hobbies contribute to personal growth.

Advice for Managerial Round:

Balance technical and non-technical aspects in your answers.
Stay confident and concise—avoid over-explaining.
Structure your responses strategically to make a strong impression.

Takeaways and Reflections

While I didn’t clear the final round, this experience taught me a lot about:

Preparation: Know your strengths, projects, and certifications thoroughly.
Presentation: Keep responses concise and impactful.
Balance: Combine technical expertise with soft skills.

For first-time interviewees, I recommend:

Practice presenting your projects and achievements.
Stay confident and familiarize yourself with your resume.
Treat every experience as a step forward—setbacks are part of growth.

experiences.title: CIS Interview Experience
experiences.full_content:

The first part of the interview had me solving coding puzzles. I had to create a basic webpage with HTML and CSS, make a dynamic user interface with JavaScript, and set up a simple API with Node.js and Express.

Design Task

Debugging Challenge

After that, I entered a virtual arena to fix bugs in a legacy codebase. I had to find and resolve as many issues as possible, including syntax errors and logical problems.

Final Interview

The last part was a video call with senior developers and managers. They asked about my past projects, problem-solving skills, and how I handle teamwork and deadlines. They also gave me hypothetical problems to solve on the spot.

Job Offer

A few days later, I received a job offer in a beautifully designed email, detailing my new role and responsibilities. The interview was challenging but exciting, and it made me feel ready for my new job as a web developer.

This interview was a fun and engaging way to show off my skills and learn more about the company.

experiences.full_content:
Eligibility Criteria

You must complete courses from NetAcad provided by the college and then register for the Ideathon.

Round 1 (Online Test)

Registered students received the test link. My test was on 25th June 2025. The test consisted of 51 MCQs and 1 coding question. The MCQs were on the topics of Python, CCNA, and aptitude. The coding question was a hard dynamic programming question. The platform for the test was HackerRank.

The result was announced after 15–20 days, on 12th July 2024. We received the results via email from the college. A total of about 360 students from across India were selected for the further rounds of interviews.

Round 2 (PPT Submission)

We were provided with 3 problem statements by Cisco on the 12th of July. We had to create a PPT solution for one of the topics. The solution did not need to be implemented; we just had to provide the solution to the problem. The PPT had to be submitted within 5 days using the link provided by Cisco in the email. The submission deadline was the 18th of July.

The next interview was scheduled for the 22nd of July.

Round 3 (Technical Round TR) (Elimination Round)

This was a virtual round on the Webex platform. The interview lasted for 1 hour. First, they asked me about myself, and then they started with questions about my projects.

Questions on Project:

1. Explain the project.

2. Why did you create this?

3. What challenges did you face?

4. Is this a team project?

5. Why didn’t you create the project with a team?

6. How is it different from other similar projects available on the internet?

Networking Questions:

1. What is the OSI model?

2. Explain each layer one by one.

3. What are the protocols of the OSI in each layer?

4. Why are both MAC and IP addresses needed?

5. How are MAC and IP addresses related?

6. What is ARP?

7. DHCP, UDP vs TCP.

8. Use of the session layer.

9. How do you rate your CCNA skills?

10. Protocols of routing.

11. Routing table.

12. How does a router work?

After that, they asked me to rate my coding skills. I said 8.

Coding Questions:

1. What is sorting and different sorting algorithms with time and space complexity?

2. What is the main function?

3. Some OOPs questions.

4. Operations of a linked list.

5. Hash map.

6. Some more questions I am unable to recall.

7. Asked me whether I was comfortable with trees or linked lists.

Then they told me to share my screen and write code. I opened the online GDB compiler.

1. Code for factorial.

2. Linked list code for implementation and operations.

After that, they told me to open my PPT that I submitted in Round 2. I presented my PPT, and they asked me many questions about it:

1. Will it work?

2. How will you do it?

3. Tech stack.

4. Many questions about the PPT.

After that, the interview was over. I asked 2 questions to them.

Out of 350 students, 200 were selected for the further rounds.

Round 4 (Manager Round MR) (Elimination Round)

The interview started with problem-solving as I had written on my resume that I have a 5 rating on HackerRank and good problem-solving skills.

Questions:

14. One more networking question that I was not able to answer.

After that, I asked some questions.

experiences.title: Cisco Ideathon Experience 2k24 | Technical Consultant Engineer.
extracted_questions: What is the OSI model?
What is the difference between a switch and a router?
What is the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)?
experiences.full_content:
Eligibility Criteria

Your college must be part of the NetAcad Platform. Additionally, you must have completed the required certifications to participate in the Cisco Ideathon. The necessary courses will be provided by your college, so communicate with your faculty who are handling the NetAcad academy for your campus.

In my case, we were enrolled in six courses. We had to finish them before the deadline to be eligible for Cisco. The following courses were offered by my college to meet the eligibility criteria:

CCNA: Introduction to Networks
CCNA: Introduction to Cybersecurity
Cisco Python Certificate
CCNA: Enterprise Networking
Based on the course completion status, my college allowed 70 students to be eligible for the Ideathon. Please note that you should not have any standing arrears or backlogs in the past.

1st Round

The first round was relatively easy. This time, they changed the pattern for the Ideathon. It consisted of 51 objective questions and 1 advanced coding question. The 51 objective questions were from the courses you completed on the NetAcad platform, covering topics like networking, cybersecurity, Python, aptitude, and other areas. The coding platform was Hacker Rank. You do not need to write the code from scratch; you will be given a complete main function, and you just have to complete the function. Practice on Hacker Rank to improve your accuracy.

2nd Round

About 20 to 25 days later, they announced the results. From my college, only 5 students cleared that round (including me). The next round was the Idea Submission round. They will email eligible candidates with problem statements. Although this round is not an elimination round, your idea should be unique and feasible. Try to incorporate Cisco tools and new products into your ideas. They will not ask for implementation, but you need to have a clear understanding of your ideas.

In my case, I selected problem statement 4 (which was about reducing the loss of personal identity like Aadhar card, PAN card, and other documents in this digital era). I created a project called "Blockchain-based Decentralized Personal Document Locker." Try to make your presentation simple and clean, using simple and professional themes. Ensure that your presentation has no more than 7-8 slides.

3rd Round

After submitting our ideas and resumes, we received our interview slots. My role was for a Technical Consulting Engineer, so I had my interview on July 23. You have to join the meeting at 8 AM and wait until they announce the results. Before that, they will email you a sheet with your interview slot and timing.

Technical Interview Experience:

My slot was at 2 PM. I waited until that time, and then they shared the link to my room. You will be interviewed by two interviewers and one mediator.

In my case, they started the interview by introducing themselves and then asked me to introduce myself. After my introduction, I was instructed to present my idea. I took about 17 to 20 minutes to explain my idea and approach. Later, they asked questions about the idea, including basic questions like why I chose this tech stack and which encryption and decryption techniques I was using. They also asked some basic questions about the project idea.

After that, they asked me to explain my resume. I explained my resume in detail. Then they asked some networking questions like:

What is the OSI model?
Explain TCP/IP.
What is the difference between a switch and a router?
Explain the structure of a MAC address.
What is the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)?
Explain how DNS works.
Explain how a VPN works.
I am good at networking, so I explained everything in depth. Later, they asked about my favorite coding language. I replied with Java (Don't say JAVA, if you are not good in it) and then they asked more than 45 questions about core Java concepts. Later, they asked the other interviewer to ask a few questions. He asked a few questions about my idea and projects, as well as about SQL and other database languages.

I got the selection result 30 minutes after my interview. (Only 3 students were selected from my college.)

4th Round

The next round was the Managerial round (on July 25). This round always seems easy, but they tend to reject most candidates in this round. So, prepare some answers, like how to respond to managerial questions. The interview lasted 30 to 35 minutes. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, and then he asked me to share my role experience in projects. I was the project lead in all my projects, so I explained that. Later, he asked about my hackathon win experience and my role in it, and what key challenges I faced, among other questions. Finally, he asked 4 managerial round questions.

I answered all questions confidently, but unfortunately, I was rejected in this round. (Only two students got selected.)

5th Round

This is the typical HR round, like in other companies. The HR will ask you to introduce yourself, then ask some HR questions like,

Why you want to join cisco.
If I am willing to relocate.
Bangalore or Pune.
Day or night shift.
Availability for internship or not.
Then they told me about the salary and the pay.
After that, I asked 2 questions and the interview was over.
After this round, they announced the results after one month. Only one student from my campus was selected.

Conclusion

Although my journey in the Cisco Ideathon came to an end in the Managerial round, it was an incredible learning experience. Each round taught me something valuable, and I am grateful for the opportunity to participate. For those of you who are planning to take part, I wish you the best of luck. Stay confident, prepare thoroughly, and most importantly, enjoy the experience. Remember, every step, whether successful or not, is a step forward in your journey

Good luck!

I was then asked to present the PPT from Round 2 and faced several questions regarding its feasibility, implementation approach, tech stack, and other aspects. The round concluded after a Q&A session. Out of 350 participants, 200 were selected for the next round.

Round 4: Manager Round (MR) (Elimination Round)
This round started with problem-solving questions based on my resume, highlighting my 5-star rating on HackerRank. The discussion included:

Real-world problems are solved through projects.
Justifications for creating projects even if similar ones exist online.
Questions on my interest in chess and Sudoku, understanding project documentation, and the Indian budget.
Scenarios on convincing someone to collaborate on a project and problem-solving approaches.
Teamwork experiences, staying updated with technology, and differences between networking devices.
This round lasted about 40-50 minutes. Out of 200 students, approximately 160 advanced to the HR round.

Round 5: HR Round
This was a brief and formal round, lasting only 5 minutes, covering:

Personal introduction.
Willingness to relocate (Bangalore or Pune).
Preferences for day or night shifts.
Availability for an internship.
They provided details about the salary and pay, and I concluded the interview by asking 3-4 questions.

Result
Results were announced 20 days later, and unfortunately, I was not selected. Only 22 students were chosen for the Technical Consulting role across all candidates from India. Notably, none of the applicants, including myself, were selected for the Consulting Engineer position, possibly due to a hiring freeze or layoffs without any explanation.

Learning
Throughout this journey, I've learned that sometimes, success depends on luck. However, navigating through the entire process was an accomplishment in itself, making me stronger and bolder. Going through all the rounds and gaining this experience is something I take pride in, regardless of the outcome.

experiences.full_content:
Every year Cisco conducts its ideation for students with potential and creativity to be a part of Cisco's team. Students who clear all the interview rounds get an Internship+FTE offer from Cisco. This year the ideation was conducted in phases. Phase 1 was for Technical Consulting Engineer, Consulting Engineer, and Software Consulting Engineer, phase 2 was for Site Reliability Engineer.

Cisco nowadays has a concept of inclusive resume where you have to prepare your resume in such a way that it should not have your college name, degree, branch, cgpa or any personal details like LinkedIn or gmail and you are also not allowed to mention any of these things in the interview. Every candidate was given a candidate code which was its identity during the whole interview process.

ELIGIBILITY

Must be a Netacad student.
All three Modules of CCNA.
All two modules of Python.
6 CGPA or above with no active backlogs.

Round 1: Online Test (elimination round)

The online test was on 25th June and was conducted on Hacker rank and we were asked to give our role preference. The format for assessment was 52 questions to be solved in 1 hour. The assessment had

8 python questions of easy-medium level
30 networking questions of medium-hard level
5 cybersecurity questions of easy level
8 Aptitude questions of easy-medium level
1 Coding question of medium level
I was able to solve most of the questions in the given time.

Results were announced after two weeks and 360 students pan India were shortlisted for the interviews and I was one of them.

Round 2: Idea Submission (non-elimination round)

All the shortlisted students were given three problem statements and tasked with creating a presentation showing their solutions. The solutions were then discussed during the interviews. We were given one week to complete the presentation, and those who submitted it before the deadline were invited for the interview.

Round 3: Technical Interview (elimination round) (1hr 40mins)

The interview started at around 12:15 pm and there were two interviewers. I greeted both of them and they did the same. They were nice and asked me whether I had my breakfast and lunch. After this the interview started and I was allowed to share my screen and present my solution. The moment I started, the interviewer stopped me and asked me why I chose this topic, after answering that I went on to explain my solutions. The interviewers were cross questioning me on almost every line that I was saying . They just wanted to test whether I was able to defend my solutions or not. The presentation went on for almost 30 mins.
After the presentation one of the interviewer went through my resume and asked me to tell him the work I did in my internship, this discussion went on for another 10-15 mins. Then they asked me my favourite coding language, to which I replied C++ but Java was also mentioned in my resume so he asked me some basic java questions like

Are there pointers in java?
Why pointers don't exist in java.
Why java is platform independent?
I was able to answer all of them

Then the interviewer asked me

What is stack memory
What is heap memory
Memory management in C++
I was able to answer all of them

After this the second interviewer took over and asked me whether I am familiar with Computer Networks to which I said yes

Then he asked me

What is OSI model
Layers of OSI model
Why we need OSI model when we have TCP/IP model
Some discussion on VPN
What is CSMA/CD
The interviewer was satisfied with my response.

He then continued to ask me some managerial type questions, he made some scenarios and asked me what I will do in these situations. The discussion went on for around 20-25 mins and finally the interview was over.
Though the interview was scheduled for 1 hour but mine went till 1 hour 40 mins.

In the evening, HR shared the list of unsuccessful candidates, and my name was not in the list. Shortly after, I received an email confirming that I had been selected for the managerial round, which was scheduled for July 26th.

Round 4: Managerial interview (elimination round) 1hr 15mins

The interview began at around 12:00 PM, with a single interviewer who was highly experienced. He was the coolest person I had ever met. He first introduced himself and asked me for my introduction without my name and other details. He was super cool he asked me about do I play games and which is my favourite game. The discussion on gaming went on for 10 mins. He then asked me to briefly tell him about my solutions that I presented in the Technical Interview. After that he asked me to explain my projects and internships.

He began by asking about the clubs I was involved with in college and the work I had done there. After that, he shifted to managerial questions, focusing on scenarios like, "Tell me about a time when..."

He also asked me questions like

Your strengths and weaknesses
What is the most difficult problem you faced and how you overcame that.
Your biggest failure
Then he started with scenario based questions and we had a long discussion on few of them.

I was not asked any technical questions in this round.

At the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked, "What is a typical day in the life of a consulting engineer?" His detailed response started a small discussion about the role, which lasted for about 7–8 minutes.

At the end he told me that I am a good candidate and he believes that I will somehow solve any problem that is given to me and he also wished me the best for the next round.

After 1 hour of waiting I was called for the ETR connect round. It was the final round with the HR of Cisco.

Round 5: ETR Connect (elimination round) (10 mins)

The interview began at around 3 PM with the HR. He mentioned that this round was not inclusive, as he already knew everything about me.

Some question he asked were:

Why you chose this college and the field of study
From where you are
Explain the app development project briefly
Are you open for relocation to Bengaluru or Pune
This job may require working late at nights or early in the morning so are you okay with that
Any Plans for higher studies
He then informed me about the internship stipend and the CTC, and mentioned that the results would be announced in three weeks.

At the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked, "Why is Cisco considered one of the best places to work?"

The interview ended.

About 2.5 weeks later, the results were announced. Out of the 160 candidates who participated in the ETR Connect, only 22 were selected, and they were chosen for Technical Consulting roles. No one was selected for Consulting Engineer or Software Consulting Engineer positions. I’m unsure why Cisco chose such a small number of candidates this year, especially after conducting HR rounds for 160 candidates.

Verdict: Not Selected

experiences.title: Cisco Interview Experience (Off-Campus 2025 Summer Internship)
experiences.full_content:
This article covers my interview experience for the Summer Internship 2025 drive by Cisco. I'll go through the overall process with the dates, and hopefully this helps y'all! :)

VERDICT: SELECTED

Applied - 25th August, 2024

I originally came across the opening on LinkedIn and applied on the Cisco Careers portal through a referral on the official Careers page.

Online Assessment - 2nd September, 2024

The assessment consisted of 2 sections.

The MCQ section:42 MCQs based on Computer Networks, OOPs, Operating Systems, DBMS, Aptitude, and Computer Fundamentals.  I personally found this section easy, and I believe this section was what led to my shortlisting as my DSA section hadn't gone too well.

The DSA section:2 Questions, one Dynamic Programming based and the other based on Graphs.

The Interview Call - 11th October, 2024

Around 12 pm, I received a call from a recruiter at Cisco informing me of my shortlisting for the interview and confirming my availability for the interview.

I was also asked to share my resume in a specific inclusive format that Cisco requires resumes to be in.

First Interview Round (Technical) - 14th October, 2024

I had my interview scheduled at 12:00 pm, and the expected duration was around 30 minutes. My interview stretched up to about 45 minutes and would've taken longer but I had an exam at 1:00 pm so we had to cut it short.  This interview was set up with a Software Engineer.

I was interviewed majorly on my previous internship experience - what my contribution to it was, and each of my projects in detail. (Make sure to know your projects in depth and able to answer any question based on it). We then delved into a basic DSA Question ( Something similar to this - Frequency of Characters in Alphabetical Order)

I didn't ask the right clarifying questions before diving into the code, so make sure you know what the expected output is before you start to come up with an approach. This led to me getting the wrong output, and the interview shifted in the direction of assessing how i would debug issues in case they arose.

There probably would have been more DSA questions, but the interview ended at this due to the time constraint.

Second Interview Round (Technical) - 22nd October, 2024

I received a mail about 4 days after the first interview that my 2nd interview was scheduled on 22nd. This was what I believe is called the Hiring Manager round, and was set up with an Engineering Leader at Cisco. This interview too, stretched upto about 45 minutes to an hour.

The interview began with my introduction, and we dove straight into questions about my favourite subject, to which I replied Networks. I was quizzed on various protocols, and where they found applications.

Next, I was asked about what data structure I would use to store an Employee Database, and the time complexity for each action on the Database.

After this, the interview steered in the direction of System Design. I had to design and develop an app that was meant to be a competitor to Instagram. I was given about 5 minutes to think it through and come up with a basic architecture. After I explained my architecture, I was asked a follow-up question about delay handling in case of distributed systems, and I wasn't able to answer it correctly as I had not dealt with such systems in the past.

The interview ended with me asking the Manager questions about the team he worked at, and what interns do in the team.

Third Interview Round (The ETR Connect Round) - 28th October, 2024

On 28th, I received a call from the recruiter asking me to schedule a 10-15 minute meeting, which I was informed was a casual connect session with the ETR ( Emerging Talent Recruitment as Cisco calls it).

This was a casual call discussing my availability for the internship and stipend and duration details. I was also asked how excited I'd be if I were to be shortlisted for the internship.

The selection mail! - 28th October, 2024

About 2 hours after the ETR round ended, I recieved a mail informing me that I had been shortlisted for the offer at Cisco for the Summer Internship 2025.

I hope this article helps future applicants understand the process better, as these helped me immensely during my preparation for the interviews! :)

experiences.full_content:
Company Name:  Citi Bank. I received a call from Naukri.

The Karat interview for SDET (Software Development Engineer in Test) typically involves a structured assessment divided into multiple sections:

Scenario-Based Testing: Questions focused on general testing principles, scenarios, and situational problem-solving.

SQL Assessment: Practical questions on SQL queries to evaluate database skills.

Selenium Evaluation: Hands-on tasks or theoretical questions to assess proficiency in Selenium.

Coding Round: A programming round to test problem-solving and coding abilities.

The total duration of the interview is usually 1 hour, with time evenly distributed across these sections.

There were a total of 4 rounds: two technical rounds, one managerial round, and the final round with the client.

1. The first 2 rounds were based on Java programming related to string and array-based programs.

2. The third round was conducted by the delivery manager. All three rounds were organized by Mphasis IT Company for their client, Citi Bank.

3. Karat took the fourth round on behalf of Citi Bank. The questions focused on

SQL

File handling in a CI/CD pipeline

Canary deployment,
how to create a pipeline,
Lift shift testing,
Blue-Green Deployment.

experiences.title: CodingMart Technologies Interview Experience On-Campus
experiences.full_content:
Hello All,

I attended the interview Conducted by CodingMart Technologies on our Campus(KIOT). It happened during the sixth semester. Majorly It consists of 4 rounds

1st round - Online Technical Round.
2nd round - Online Pogramming Round.
3rd round - Technical Discussion/Presentation.
4th round - HR Discussion.

1st Round

Before the first round, there will be a pre-placement talk on the interview process from the technical team and HR team of CodingMart Technologies.

In the first round, you will be asked to complete the Technical MCQs on DataStructures and Algorithms and basic Programming logic-based Questions. They will set some cut-off marks. you have to score minimum 75 %(not sure) in that test.

2nd Round

The second round will be your Programming round. You can use Java, C++, C, and Python to complete the test. There will be 5 sets of questions. Each set contains only 1 Question. The Question will be in a Medium to Hard Range. The question that I faced was "Ballon Burst" (Available Online). They will give you 5 - 10 min for preparation. You may use online to refer to the Questions(they won't allow you to use ChatGPT). After that, you have to solve the problem and you have to explain the approach that you used to solve the problem to the CodingMart Team. After that, they will give some additional enhancement to your problem, and then you have to solve the problem and explain the approach. If you complete the given problem and the Enhancement, you can easily clear the 2nd round.

3rd Round

The third round will be a Technical Discussion. In this Round, you will be given a presentation topic, you have to prepare for the topic (They will give the topic one day before your interview) and you have to present it to the technical team. Then you have to showcase your project to the HRs and be ready with your projects, mostly they will focus on projects and ask for some programming problems to solve. If you perform well, you can easily clear this round.

4th Roud

The Fourth Round will be the General HR. In this round, they will ask about your family, your hobbies, your strengths and weaknesses. You can easily clear this round. If you clear the Technical round, surely you will be selected by CodingMart Technologies.

Finally, That was a good experience and this was an overall interview process for CodingMart Technologies.

experiences.title: Codingmart Technologies Interview Experience | SDE Role | Coimbatore | Bangalore
experiences.full_content:
About Codingmart

Codingmart was a service-based company founded in 2012. Codingmart transitioned to a private limited company in 2015, offering top-tier IT consulting to Indian unicorns like Ola, BookMyShow, Nykaa, and Udaan. Based in Coimbatore with a key development center, Codingmart serves diverse sectors with elite talent from South Indian campuses. Codingmart's rigorous 3 + 1 round recruitment process maintains a 0.5% interview-to-hire ratio, ensuring high standards. With 150 exceptional talents, Codingmart achieves a remarkable 120% annual growth rate, prioritizing premium IT solutions. Working closely with top companies such as Cleartrip, Codingmart stands out in providing technology solutions for Indian consumers and business brands, contributing to the advancement of the tech industry.

About the Role and Package:

The role they looked for is a SDE intern role. They expected a person who is enthusiastic about learning, has proficient problem-solving skills, and has some basic knowledge about software development. They preferred candidates who had strong foundational knowledge of JavaScript.  They offered a package of 4.2 LPA (INR), which comes up with a two-year service agreement. This service agreement also disclaims about travelling abroad for future on-site projects if needed. The service agreement doesn't include the internship time period. At the time of the internship, you were paid 12,000 INR per month. Food and accommodations will not be provided at the time of the internship and service agreement. There is a chance of firing you at the time of the internship by considering your performance.

Interview Process of Codingmart:

You have to clear four rounds to get a job at Codingmart Technologies. All the interview rounds are mostly focused on the technical skills of the candidate. Let's discuss those rounds one by one in this post.

Round 1—Technical MCQ: This is the first round to get into codingmart technologies. It consists of 20 MCQ questions, which mainly focus on Java. You are given 45 minutes to solve those MCQ questions. These questions are not too tough. If you have some clear understanding about computer programming and Java, then you can clear this round. It was an online assessment where you can't switch between tabs. So be careful before attending this round. You can prepare for this round by visiting Interviewbit (https://www.interviewbit.com/java-mcq).

Round 2—Programming Round: This round is to check your problem-solving skills. It is for 45 minutes. It consists of only one programming question. You are given time to surf the internet after you receive your question. You can look for an approach to solve the problem at the time. Don't try to memorize the solution because it doesn't help you if the HR adds some extra scenarios. You need to explain your approach to the HR after you write the code. This is the most important thing at this round. If they are not satisfied with your approach, then they assume you were copied from the internet. You can prepare for this round by visiting GeeksForGeeks.

Round 3—Technical Presentation: This round is to check your presentation skills and technical knowledge about domains. In this round, you are allotted a domain and a topic. You need to prepare a presentation slide to present about the topic for 15 minutes with 6 to 10 slides.

Round 4—Technical HR: It was a face-to-face interview round where your technical knowledge was assessed. This round is a crucial one to get your offer at Codingmart Technologies. In this round, most of the questions are about your resume, core concepts and OOPS concepts of Java, and basic SQL queries. You can also prepare yourself to answer the questions on some concepts like computer networks, operating systems, etc. Answering questions with confidence will definitely increase your chance to get the offer.

Conclusion:

I hope this post will help you to have some understanding about recruitment process of Codingmart technologies. Always prepare your best for the interview. Don't panic if you can't answer a question or recall something. Be confident while answering questions. Try to interact with the HR by asking some insightful doubts and clarifications. But remember, don't irritate them by asking for sake questions. Always ask for the name of HR if they haven't introduced themselves. Asking their name will definitely register your face or name to them in a positive manner. Don't get disappointed if you don't get an offer; take that as an experience and learn from your mistakes. All the best for your interviews. Happy coding!!!

experiences.title: Cognizant Digital Nurture Program 3.0 Interview Experience
experiences.full_content:
In May 2024, I embarked on the Cognizant Digital Nurture Program 3.0 for Salesforce, aimed at training candidates for GenC and GenC Pro roles. The program, designed for aspiring Salesforce developers, consisted of multiple rounds to rigorously screen, train, and evaluate candidates.

Application and Initial Rounds

The application process began through Superset, where I submitted my details for the Salesforce track. Shortly after, I received an invitation to participate in a communication skills assessment in May. This round was an elimination round, testing not just communication ability but clarity of expression and how well I could communicate complex ideas simply, which is a critical skill for client-facing roles.

Upon passing the communication round, I advanced to the technical round held in July. This round was designed to assess fundamental coding skills, SQL knowledge, and web development basics. It comprised:

- Two coding questions that required problem-solving skills; while the difficulty was moderate, it allowed flexibility in approach, and candidates could modify solutions to optimize for efficiency.

- Two SQL questions that tested data manipulation and query optimization. These were moderate to hard in difficulty.

- Multiple-choice questions on web development, focusing on core concepts in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

This technical round served as a significant elimination stage, allowing Cognizant to ensure that only candidates with a foundational understanding of programming and database concepts advanced to the intensive training phase.

Deep Skilling Phase

After clearing the technical round, I was admitted into the Deep Skilling phase, a five-week immersive training program centered on Salesforce learning modules available on the Trailhead platform. This phase provided a structured yet hands-on learning experience, ensuring each candidate had a working grasp of Salesforce fundamentals by the end. Each week we were assigned a new module covering aspects of Salesforce, from CRM basics to data models, automation, and application development.

This phase also included:

1. Coach Connect Sessions - Held every Monday and Friday, these sessions allowed us to interact with mentors and coaches who guided us on that week’s learning goals. They provided tips on navigating Trailhead and efficiently completing assessments.

2. SME Connects - Once a week, a Subject Matter Expert (SME) session was conducted. This session allowed us to discuss more complex or technical topics with Salesforce experts, who provided detailed insights into the practical aspects of Salesforce development. These sessions proved invaluable in understanding the nuances of certain topics and in handling projects.

Each week’s module came with a list of projects and assessments that were essential for collecting badges. In total, I earned 39 badges by completing the required modules, projects, and assessments. This badge requirement acted as a milestone for us to measure our progress and demonstrated our ability to use Trailhead effectively.

By early September, I successfully submitted all 39 badges, meeting the program’s submission requirements.

Interview Process

In September, eligible candidates were notified via email that they qualified for the interview phase. Our interviews were initially scheduled for late September, but this was rescheduled to two days later, and were to be conducted at the Cognizant office.

On the interview day, I arrived at the Cognizant office by 7:30 AM. Due to the high number of candidates, the wait time was long, but the on-site team managed the process well. Around midday, I was finally called in for my interview, which was conducted by two technical interviewers.

My interview experience was comprehensive and spanned approximately 40-45 minutes. Here’s how it unfolded:

-Introduction: I was asked to introduce myself, during which I provided an overview of my background, my interest in Salesforce, and my experience with the Trailhead projects.

-Salesforce-Specific Questions: The interviewers inquired about my familiarity with Salesforce and asked questions on CRM fundamentals, Salesforce data structures, and automation processes like workflows and triggers. I highlighted my experience from the Trailhead projects, where I had applied some of these features hands-on. This consisted about 70% of my interview.

-Technical Topics in OOP and DBMS: I mentioned OOPS and DBMS as my favorite subjects in my resume. So they asked me questions on Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts. Questions were from from fundamental principles like abstraction and encapsulation. Additionally, they asked about Database Management Systems (DBMS), SQL commands, and relational database concepts, testing my understanding of data structuring and query optimization.

-HR Questions: To assess my cultural fit and interpersonal skills, the interviewers included a few HR-style questions. They asked about my motivations for choosing Salesforce as a career path, how I handle challenges in a collaborative environment, whether i would be okay relocating to some other place, or whether i would be okay in any other domain, and my goals for professional growth.

Throughout the interview, I aimed to provide detailed answers and demonstrate how my Trailhead experience had prepared me for real-world applications of Salesforce. The interviewers provided encouraging feedback, especially about my practical understanding of Salesforce modules and my ability to communicate technical concepts clearly.

Results

The results were declared on late October and I was thrilled to learn that I had been selected for the GenC Pro role.

My Experience with ITPT Off-Campus Placements via Superset

I recently had the opportunity to participate in the ITPT off-campus placements specifically designed for 3-year graduates, conducted through the Superset platform. The process was divided into three phases, each designed to evaluate different skills.

Phase 1: Communication Assessments

The first round was focused on assessing our communication skills, which included:

Reading: Understanding and interpreting written content.

Writing: Conveying thoughts clearly and coherently.

Thinking: Analyzing situations and forming logical conclusions.

Listening: Comprehending spoken information accurately.

Phase 2: Aptitude Assessment

The second round tested our problem-solving abilities through various quantitative and logical reasoning questions. The topics covered were:

Percentage

Profit and Loss

Simple Interest

Time and Work

Time and Distance

Ages

Data Interpretation: Questions based on Pie charts and Bar graphs.

Phase 3: Technical Interview

The final phase was a face-to-face technical interview held at the Cognizant office, coordinated via the Superset platform. Here’s a brief overview of how it went:

Panelist: Introduce yourself.

Me: Answered confidently, highlighting my background and key achievements.

Panelist: Tell me about your school and PU college.

Me: Shared details about my educational journey.

Panelist: Describe your academic project.

Me: Explained the project’s objectives, methodology, and outcomes.

Panelist: What challenges did you face during the project?

Me: Discussed the obstacles encountered and how I overcame them.

Panelist: What is RDBMS, and why is it used instead of DBMS?

Me: Provided a detailed explanation, highlighting the advantages of RDBMS in real-time applications.

Panelist: Where can you find RDBMS in real-time scenarios?

Me: Gave examples of real-world applications where RDBMS is implemented.

The panelist then asked me to solve a few problems in the chatbox:

Palindrome Program: Demonstrated my coding skills.

Linear and Non-Linear Data Structures: Explained the concepts.

Aptitude Questions: Answered questions on Time and Work, and Direction Sense.

Garbage Collection in Java: Discussed Java’s memory management.

Panelist: Are you ready to relocate?

Me: Yes, sir.

Panelist: Do you have any questions for me?

Me: Asked insightful questions about the work culture and the tech stacks predominantly used at Cognizant.

Key Takeaways

The interview process emphasized the importance of staying calm and confident. It’s crucial to answer questions honestly and thoughtfully. For those preparing for similar interviews, focus on your communication skills, aptitude, and technical knowledge. And don’t forget to inquire about the company culture—it shows your genuine interest.

Best of luck with your upcoming interviews!

experiences.full_content:
Before the interview, I went through several stages of the Cognizant Digital Nurture program. My interview took place in person with two interviewers—one HR representative was present physically, while the other joined via the Superset platform. I logged into Superset before the interview started. Both HR representatives had technical expertise, leading to very few HR questions; the interview was primarily a combination of HR and technical assessments.

Interview Date: September 27, 2024
Duration: 40-45 minutes

The entire interview session was recorded on the Superset platform, which also features built-in online compilers and interpreters for various languages, including SQL, Java, C++, and Python. Since I was interviewing for the Java Full Stack Engineer role, I chose to code in Java, even though I practice DSA primarily in C++.

Interview Structure

Introduction:The interview began with a brief introduction from my side.

Technical Questions:OOP Concepts:Discussed the four pillars of OOP.
Asked about different access modifiers.
Explained inheritance and its various forms in Java.
Provided a real-life scenario to illustrate polymorphism.

Major Project:Briefly described my major project, mentioning it was still in progress.

Internship Discussion:Discussed my internship with no cross-questions.

Resume Projects:Answered questions regarding the tech stacks mentioned in my resume. (O)
Explained what Spring/Spring Framework is. (O)

Coding Tasks:The interviewers requested coding tasks in Java, observing how efficiently I wrote the code:Write a code to print all the factors of the number 9.
Reverse the string "Your_Name".
Swap two numbers without using a third variable and again without using addition or subtraction (using the XOR operator).
Find the largest and second-largest numbers in the array. (O)

Database Questions:Discussed the Collection framework and its usage in my projects.
Answered questions about SQL, including:The difference between DBMS and RDBMS.
Writing a query to fetch the second highest salary from the employee table, explaining the logic.
Writing a query to fetch the first three letters of every row in the "Name" column from the employee table, along with an explanation.

SQL Query Challenges:I was given a table schema and asked to code five queries in the compiler:Find names starting with "A".
Find different departments in the table.
Count the number of employees in each department.
Retrieve names of employees who participated in any events (joining another table where EmpID is the primary key).
Write a query to select the first four letters of all names in the column, resulting in names like SHYA, SWET, RAHU, etc.

Further Technical Questions:What is MVC?
How is Spring Boot different from Spring?
Discussed the differences between Delete, Truncate, and Drop, and provided some DDL commands. (O)

Confirmed my willingness to relocate and work night shifts.
I was invited to ask any questions.

Result Date: October 23, 2024
Verdict: Selected for the GenC Next package.

Note: Most interviewees were asked Spring-related questions, whereas I had fewer inquiries on that topic, despite my training in Spring, Hibernate, Spring Boot, and REST API. Out of 54 interviewees, 35 were selected, with 6 for the GenC NEXT role and the rest for the GenC role. It’s essential to study thoroughly during the Deep Skilling Round to secure a Next Role.

Tips for Success:

Avoid mentioning unnecessary details on your resume or Superset, as questions can stem from those areas. Even a single tech stack you're unfamiliar with can lead to rejection.
Interviewers often look for any mistakes, so be prepared for probing questions.
Explain your code as you write it; this gives you an edge.
Prepare a solid introduction and aim to impress in the first 10 minutes.
If you don't know an answer, move on confidently to the next question.
Maintain a positive demeanor throughout the interview.

experiences.title: Cognizant Interview Experience for Software Engineer
experiences.full_content:
One crisp autumn morning, I received an email from Cognizant inviting me for an interview. The subject line read: "Interview Invitation – Software Engineer." My heart raced; after weeks of preparation—polishing my technical skills, practicing problem-solving, and researching the company’s culture—this was the moment I had been waiting for. I had heard about Cognizant’s rigorous interview process, but I was ready to face it head-on.

The Arrival

Upon arrival at the Cognizant office, a modern building towering against the city skyline, I was welcomed by a receptionist who handed me a visitor's pass and directed me to the interview floor. The atmosphere was vibrant, filled with the hum of people working and the clicks of keyboards—a true hub of innovation and teamwork.

In the lobby, I joined a group of other candidates, some reviewing their resumes while others discussed coding challenges. The energy was a mix of anticipation and excitement. As my interview time approached, a recruiter called me in, and the journey began.

The Technical Round

Entering the interview room, I was greeted by two interviewers—a senior software engineer and a hiring manager—who introduced themselves, projecting a balanced blend of professionalism and approachability.

The senior engineer started with a problem: “You’re given an array of integers. Find the longest subarray with a sum equal to zero.” Taking a moment to collect my thoughts, I explained my approach using a hash map to track cumulative sums and identify the longest subarray with a zero sum. As I worked through the solution on the whiteboard, I could see them nodding in approval.

The hiring manager then asked, “How would you optimize this solution?” I proposed an alternative using a sliding window approach and a deque to manage maximum and minimum sums, which seemed to impress them. We continued with a discussion on edge cases and handling large inputs, covering time complexity and space optimization.

The HR Round

After the technical round, I was escorted to meet the HR manager. She welcomed me warmly, asking about my background, my reasons for wanting to join Cognizant, and how I envisioned my role in the company.

“Tell me about a time you faced a challenging project and how you handled it,” she prompted.

I shared an experience from a recent internship, where I tackled a complex application debugging challenge under tight deadlines. I explained how teamwork, resilience, and time management helped us meet the goal. She nodded approvingly, commenting, “You seem to have a strong team spirit, which is something we value at Cognizant.”

When asked about my future aspirations, I expressed a desire to continually learn, tackle complex problems, and eventually lead projects that impact real-world applications. We discussed Cognizant’s growth in AI and the company’s commitment to continuous learning, which aligned perfectly with my goals.

The Wait

I was informed to expect a response in a week. The following days felt like an eternity as I refreshed my inbox repeatedly. Each passing moment was filled with anticipation, yet I was content knowing I had done my best.

Finally, one morning, an email appeared in my inbox:

“Congratulations! We are pleased to offer you the position of Software Engineer at Cognizant.”

I reread it several times, my heart pounding with joy. The countless hours spent studying algorithms and solving coding challenges had paid off.

The Offer and Joining

After accepting the offer, the onboarding process was smooth, and soon I was at the office, surrounded by brilliant minds eager to learn and contribute. My first project involved developing a web application for a healthcare client, using the latest technologies and agile practices. It was inspiring to see how our work could have a tangible impact on people's lives.

With time, I realized that Cognizant was more than just a workplace—it was an environment where I could grow, innovate, and thrive. The culture of collaboration, emphasis on skill development, and commitment to impactful solutions made it an ideal fit for me.

Moral of the Story

The Cognizant interview process was challenging, embodying the company’s commitment to excellence and growth. Success required more than technical knowledge; it demanded strong communication, critical thinking, and adaptability. Receiving the offer was just the beginning of an exciting journey in the world of technology.

Where do you see yourself in five years?
Are you open to working in multiple locations?
Are you open to working day and night shifts?

Final Thoughts

The interview was conducted in a friendly and professional manner, making it an enjoyable experience. The interviewer showed genuine interest in understanding both my technical expertise and personal preferences.

For future aspirants:

Be thorough with your primary programming language (e.g., Java, Python).
Have a good understanding of SQL basics and be ready to write queries.
Practice problem-solving for basic coding challenges.
Be honest and confident during the HR round.
Overall, it was a pleasant and insightful process.

experiences.title: Cognizant Interview Experience | GENC Next
experiences.full_content:
I was selected for the GenC Next role at Cognizant with an annual compensation of 6.75 LPA. The interview process revolved around the skill cluster I chose, which included C#, SQL, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The Screening Process

The screening process was conducted prior to the interview, and I was called in for the interview about two hours later. The interview was conducted on the Superset platform, which provided an integrated IDE for coding. Two interviewers participated in the process:

One interviewer was physically present.
The other joined virtually.

Technical Questions and Tasks

Coding Task

I was given a simple problem: Count the even integers in an array.

I was allowed to choose between C, C++, or C# to implement the solution.

OOP Concepts

I was asked about the following Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts:

Polymorphism and Inheritance: I explained these with examples and discussed their types.

APIs and Front-End Technologies

I was asked about my understanding of APIs and front-end technologies. I honestly admitted that I had a basic understanding of these topics.

SQL Questions

The interview included several SQL-related questions:

1. Definitions:

Primary Key
Composite Primary Key
Normalization
Indexes
Difference between Left Join and Inner Join

2. SQL Queries:

Retrieve the top 5 employees with the highest salary from an employee table.
Retrieve the name of the employee with the maximum and minimum salary.

Behavioral and Formal Questions

Willingness to relocate
Availability to work in any shift

experiences.title: Cognizant Interview  Experience | Programmer Analyst Trainee | On-Campus Hire
experiences.full_content:
About Cognizant - Cognizant is a global professional services company that provides a broad range of services in technology and consulting, helping businesses to transform and operate effectively in the digital age. Cognizant is one of the biggest names in the IT services industry, especially well-known in India. Though it’s headquartered in the U.S. (New Jersey), a huge part of its workforce and operations are based in India. India is a major hub for Cognizant, with offices in cities like Chennai, Pune, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Kolkata.

So I have gone through Cognizant hiring for 2024 as a fresher on-campus round. I am putting these things here so that it might help other people in this community.

In Cognizant, first while registering we were given 2 cluster options of skill set:

1. Cluster 1:  Java, ANSI SQL, HTML, CSS, Javascript
2. Cluster 2: ANSI SQL, Python, Cloud Fundamentals
I chose Cluster 2.

First Round- Communication

So first round was the Communication Round which lasted for about 40-45 minutes. It is easy to medium level. In one section you have to repeat what is written on the screen. In another section you will hear an audio recording, you have to repeat it. In last section you have to speak about a topic given by them for 1 minute, you will be given 30 seconds to think about the topic. Like this, there are a few more sections that are fairly easy.

Second Round - Aptitude Assessment + Technical Assessment

The second round was Aptitude assessment + Technical Assessment. So as I chose cluster 2, there was a coding round in Python that had 2 questions and the level was easy to medium. And in another section, we had to write SQL queries. There already was a database, I was given  2 questions in this. The level of questions was easy to medium. In the third section, there was an MCQ about cloud fundamentals.

Aptitude assessment and technical assessment took place on 2 consecutive days. First, the aptitude assessment took place and the next day technical assessment took place. So I think the marks here are cumulatively calculated.

Third Round - Technical Interview

The third was a technical interview round in-person. The interviewer was quite friendly. So the interview started with a "Tell me about yourself" question. Then I had some questions from my resume about my skills and projects. One of the questions was the difference between Excel and Power BI. Then he asked me to write some DDL command syntax and asked some questions related to SQL like normalization and explain with example. Then he asked me about cloud fundamentals. And one question I clearly remember was how would I explain cloud technology to a non-tech person to which I gave really an impressing answer and I myself was not expecting to give such a good answer as my domain was not in Cloud at all. So the interview was pretty much a cake walk for me.

And I received my LOI in about 2-3 weeks later.

Conclusion and Suggestion-

Atleast have basic knowledge about every skill in the cluster you choose.
Practice easy to medium programming question on any coding site.
Practice coomunication, sometimes your good communication can also save you.
Be formal dressed for the interview.
Take your laptop as well to the venue because though the interview was in-person, we were asked to login to superset and our video recording was done through that.

experiences.title: Cohesity Interview Experience for Site Reliability Engineer role On-Campus(2024)
experiences.full_content:
In this post I shall be sharing my placement experience at Cohesity India for the SRE role. About 250 students had registered and the whole process was finished in a single day. The process took place on 30th September 2024.

Role: Site Reliability Engineer (SRE)

Role Offered: Yes

Role Type: Only Full Time

Total Number of Candidates selected : 4

Round 1 (Online Assessment) :

Questions were mainly from OS, CN, Linux and Cloud. There were also a few Aptitude questions in the mix.
The platform used was Codesignal.
The test consisted of 45 MCQs in 30 minutes so speed was very crucial along with accuracy but there was no negative marking
Round 2 (Technical Round 1) :

A total of 25 people were selected for the next round and it was face to face interviews.
There were no DSA questions asked in this round as it was for an SRE role.
There were questions about file systems like which file system is used in Windows, Linux, etc.
A few questions were also asked about OS and CN like the OSI model, etc.
The questions were quite easy but it tested your fundamentals so better to revise your core concepts once before entering the interview.
Round 3 (Technical Round 2) :

A few people were let go after the first round but not sure of the number.
The same concepts as listed above were tested in this round as well.
Fundamental questions on core concepts like DHCP and hardware troubleshooting using Linux commands were tested in this round which could only be answered by having a clear understanding of the concepts.
Questions were asked about my system like what configuration it has and stuff like that so be ready to answer such questions.
Round 4 (HR Round) :

This was a small behavioral round, consisting of scenario-based questions like, "What would you do if you had a bad manager?" These questions were aimed at checking how you would respond to certain situations in a corporate environment.
My advice for this round is do not search up any top 50 HR round questions online and go in instead just try to be super honest with your answers and they will definitely be impressed.
There will obviously be no technical questions asked in this round but there can be a few exceptions sometimes so beware.
This round was just about testing who you are as a person so try to potray yourself nicely as this can be a make or break decision for hiring you. This round went on for about 30 minutes.
Conclusion:

Overall I would say this was one of the best interviews I had ever sat for considering the enthusiasm from the interviewers and the kind of questions they had asked were right in line with what was to be expected for an SRE role interview. The interviewers were all highly experienced SREs who have been working Cohesity for a very long time and have a deep understanding of what the role actually is so they could test me and the other candidates to the perfect extent.

experiences.title: Colgate Global Business Services Interview Experience | Internship | On-Campus 2022-23
experiences.full_content:
Colgate came to our campus to hire third-year students for a two-month summer internship.

The first round was a cognitive assessment conducted on the AON platform, consisting of 60 questions to be completed in 60 minutes. The eligibility criteria were 60% and above in all academic records. They might have also conducted resume screening, as they collected our resumes before the test. Around 30 students were selected. The stipend for the role was 25k.

The next round was held offline on the college campus. It was a group discussion (GD). Groups were formed by them, and topics were assigned to each group. In a group of around 10 people, 3 were selected. If you spoke first and had good points on the topic, your chances of getting selected increased. Just make sure you speak well, present good points, do not interrupt others while speaking, and be professional.

After this round, around 9 students were selected for an in-person interview. A panel of three Colgate interviewers, including an HR professional, conducted the interview. This was also the last round. Questions were asked based on the resume, so make sure not to include anything in the resume that you do not understand. As I mentioned in my resume I knew Excel, the interviewer asked me a few questions about Excel. Then they asked questions about extracurricular activities, the type of project I would like to work on, and other general HR questions.Also, there is a good chance of you getting selected if you know Data analysis and that stuff.

Among the 9 students, only three were selected for the internship. The result was announced on the same day.

experiences.title: Colorplast Interview Experience for the Software Engineer Role
experiences.full_content:
I had the opportunity to interview for the Software Engineer role at Colorplast Company, which visited our campus for placements. The recruitment process consisted of four rounds, and the required skills included proficiency in C/C++ and Java. Here's a detailed account of my Interview experience:

Round 1: Aptitude & Coding Test

Date: 14th November 2024

Mode: Organized on the college premises

Format:

Aptitude: 50 questions covering quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, and verbal ability.
Coding: 3 problems hosted on HackerRank, testing algorithmic skills and logical thinking.
This round was challenging but manageable. The key to success here was balancing speed and accuracy. Out of 130 students, 40 were shortlisted, and I was delighted to be one of them.

Round 2: Technical Round

Date: 27th November 2024

Mode: In-person interview with a technical panel

Format:

A mix of coding and conceptual questions. Candidates were asked to write code logic on paper and explain it.
Resume-based questions and discussions about projects.
Questions I Was Asked:

Coding Question: Check if two given sentences rhyme or not. I explained the logic and how to compare the ending sounds of both sentences.
Project Discussion: They asked in-depth questions about my projects, focusing on implementation details, challenges faced, and outcomes.
This round was more about clarity of thought and logical explanation than coding syntax. From this round, only 20 students were selected, and I was one of them.

Round 3: Technical/Personal Interview

Mode: Technical and Personal Interaction

Format:

Questions from the resume and projects.
Personal questions to understand the candidate better.
This round tested both technical skills and communication abilities. They dug deeper into my projects and asked how I approached challenges and implemented solutions. Personal questions focused on strengths, weaknesses, and career goals.

Out of 20 students, 15 were shortlisted, and I was thrilled to progress to the final round.

Round 4: HR Round

Mode: One-on-one interview with the HR representative

Format:

Questions about projects, technical concepts, and some HR-focused discussions.
Logical and bitwise operator questions.

Questions I Was Asked:

1. Bitwise Operator: Explain the difference between `~0` (bitwise NOT) and `!0` (logical NOT).

Answer:

`~0` flips all bits of 0, resulting in `-1` (in two's complement representation).

`!0` checks the logical NOT of 0, resulting in `1` (true).

2. Basic HR questions about adaptability, teamwork, and future aspirations.

After careful evaluation, 5 students were selected for the Software Engineer role, and I was one of the finalists!

Key Takeaways:

1. Preparation: Brush up on your basics in C/C++, Java, and problem-solving. Focus on projects you’ve worked on, as they play a critical role in technical rounds.

2. Clarity and Communication: Being able to explain your logic clearly is as important as writing code.

3. Confidence: Stay calm and confident, especially during personal interviews and HR discussions.

This entire experience was enriching and gave me valuable insights into cracking campus placement interviews. I’m incredibly grateful to Colorplast for this opportunity and hope my journey helps other aspirants prepare for similar roles!

experiences.title: Consultadd Interview experience (On-campus)
experiences.full_content:
Consultadd visited our college to offer the role of Associate Software Engineer. The recruitment process consisted of an online assessment followed by three rounds: two technical rounds and one techno-managerial round. Each round was elimination-based. Here's a detailed breakdown of the experience.

ROUND 1: Online Assessment (Coding Round)

The first round was a coding challenge:

Structure:

2 Medium-Level Coding Questions: Candidates were required to write the code and provide a dry run explanation for each problem based on the test case provided.

Tips to Clear This Round:

Be confident in your coding skills and dry run explanations.
Practice medium-level coding problems on platforms like LeetCode or HackerRank.

ROUND 2: Technical Round 1

This was the first technical interview, focusing on databases, problem-solving, and OOPs concepts.

Key Questions and Topics:

1. Profile Overview: Walkthrough of my profile.

2. SQL Queries: Write SQL queries using aggregate functions such as AVG and COUNT.

3. ER Diagram:

Given a company scenario, design an ER Diagram.
Include all details and relationships between tables.
4. Normalization and Joins:

Questions on normal forms and database joins.
5. Types of Keys: Explanation of primary keys, foreign keys, etc.

6. DSA Problem:

Solve a medium-level problem on strings.
Explain the approach clearly and write a pseudo-code.

Theoretical Concepts:

OOPs: Runtime polymorphism, sorting, and related concepts.

Tips to Clear This Round:

Have a solid understanding of SQL, DBMS, and OOPs concepts.
Clearly explain the approach and logic behind coding solutions.
Practice designing ER Diagrams and solving medium-level DSA problems.

ROUND 3: Technical Round 2 (Advanced Technical Interview)

This round dived deeper into technical skills, projects, and problem-solving abilities.

Key Questions and Topics:

1. Introduction: Walkthrough of technical skills, projects, and internship experiences.

2. Project-Based Questions:

Discussed challenges faced and contributions during previous internships.
Detailed explanation of Flutter-based projects, including problem statements and solutions.
3. SQL Queries:

Write medium-level queries covering self joins, nested queries, and LIMIT.
Normalize a table violating a normal form.
4. Algorithm and DSA:

Explanation of merge sort and its applications.
Solve a medium-level coding question on strings using the sliding window technique.
5. Core Concepts:

Spanning Trees, Hashing, and Heaps (e.g., insertion in a min-heap).
Runtime Polymorphism: Method overloading, method overriding, and late binding.
6. C++ Debugging:

Analyzed 2–3 C++ codes to identify errors and violations of programming concepts.

Tips to Clear This Round:

Write optimized code and explain your logic clearly.
Be prepared to discuss your projects in-depth.
Brush up on advanced SQL queries, sorting algorithms, and core computer science concepts.

ROUND 4: Techno-Managerial Round

This round evaluated both technical skills and behavioral aspects.

Key Questions and Topics:

1. Introduction:

Why I chose engineering.
My internship experiences and achievements.
2. Coding Challenge:

Solve a recursion-based problem and explain the output step-by-step.
3. Brainstorming DBMS Question:

A schema-based question requiring strong observational skills and SQL knowledge.
4. Behavioral Questions:

My extracurricular activities.
Work preferences (e.g., preferred shift and willingness to relocate).

Tips to Clear This Round:

Be confident and positive in your responses.
Pay close attention to details in tricky DBMS questions.
Ask thoughtful questions about the company to show genuine interest.

Outcome

The result was announced the same day, and I was thrilled to be selected for the role of Associate Software Engineer!

Key Takeaways

Preparation:

Practice coding problems (easy to medium level) and SQL queries on platforms like GeeksforGeeks or LeetCode.
Strengthen your understanding of DBMS and OOPs concepts.

Communication:

Clearly explain your thought process during coding and problem-solving.
Be articulate and confident while discussing projects and experiences.

Confidence:

Maintain a positive attitude and engage actively in each round.

Final Words:

The placement process was both challenging and enriching. With proper preparation and a confident mindset, you can crack it. Best of luck for your journey!

experiences.full_content:
Degree: Final year Engineering student in Information Technology
University: SGSITS Indore

Overview:

Yesterday, I participated in the interview process conducted by ConsultAdd, which was specifically for CS/IT students. Below, I outline my experience throughout the various rounds of the interview.

Interview Process:

Initial Coding Test:The first round was an online coding test, resembling a pen-and-paper format rather than a traditional IDE.
Structure:Duration: 30 minutes for coding, followed by a 5-minute dry run for each question.
Questions: There were 2 coding questions categorized as easy to medium.
Environment: The platform was similar to Notepad, and there was no compiler to run the code. They emphasized that syntax errors were not a concern; they focused on understanding my approach.

I successfully cleared this round.

Technical Interview 1:Following the online assessment, I attended Technical Interview 1.
Participants: Out of 100+ students, 54 qualified for this round, with only 12 advancing to the next stage (Technical Interview 2 + HR).
Timing: The interview process started at 10 AM and concluded at approximately 6 PM. I was the last candidate interviewed, and there were four panels conducting interviews simultaneously. Each interview lasted about 25-30 minutes.

Technical Interview Insights:

The questions covered a broad range of topics including OOP, DBMS, DSA, SQL, OS, and language-specific queries (Java in my case). No questions were repeated among the 54 students.

Questions Asked:

Introduction:The interview began with a brief introduction.

Project Discussion:I was asked to elaborate on projects mentioned in my resume. Specifically, I explained my role in a group project, the team size, any conflicts encountered, and how I managed dependencies with the backend.

Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA):I received two DSA questions:Question 1: Given an n x n matrix filled with zeros and ones, find the maximum size square that can be formed using only 1’s.Approach: I proposed two methods. The interviewer found my first recursive approach unsatisfactory and suggested optimizing it. My second approach, using the spiral method, met with approval.

Question 2: Sort an array of size n containing only the values 1, 2, and 3 in a single pass.Approach: I initially suggested four methods, but the interviewer prompted me to solve it using a two-pointer technique.

SQL Questions:I was asked about the databases I have worked with, specifically SQL.Question: How would you remove duplicate entries from a database table with constraints on primary keys and not creating a new database?I partially answered but was guided to refine my response further, including using aggregation functions.

Follow-up Questions:Difference between DISTINCT and UNIQUE keywords.
Can tables be created without a primary key? If yes, how?
Difference between primary key and unique key.

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Questions:The interviewer queried about my primary programming language (Java) and asked:What is inheritance, and how is it implemented in Java?
Explain polymorphism and provide examples of method overloading and overriding. I provided implementations and explained the differences between calling methods from parent and child classes.

Conclusion:

Overall, the interview was comprehensive, challenging, and provided an opportunity to showcase my technical knowledge. I received feedback that while my confidence and communication were commendable, I needed to focus on delivering more optimized solutions from the start to the end of my responses. I appreciated the interviewer’s guidance on refining my approach and was encouraged by their positive remarks regarding my performance.

experiences.title: Coral Telecom Interview Experience | Software Engineer | Full Time
experiences.full_content:
I’m excited to share my interview experience at Coral Telecom for a Software Engineer role. The process consisted of multiple rounds designed to assess technical knowledge, problem-solving abilities, and overall compatibility with the organization.

1. Aptitude Test

The paper-based test included 50 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) to be completed within 30 minutes.
The focus was entirely on general aptitude, with no questions on Computer Science fundamentals.
A minimum score of 25 was required to qualify for the next round.
Note: If you'd like, I can provide a general idea of the types of questions asked based on my experience.

2. Technical Interview

This round was divided into several sections and conducted by a panel of 2–3 interviewers.

i) Programming Language Basics

The interviewers assessed my knowledge of the programming language I was most comfortable with.

Since I chose Java, they asked questions on:

Core concepts: static keyword, collections, main function and its return type, HashMap vs. HashSet, Integer vs. int, Wrapper classes, objects and classes.
Advanced topics: Differences between Java 1.8 and the latest versions, lambda expressions vs. streams, Java vs. C++.
Scenario-based question: "If you were to build a transaction management microservice, which language (Java or C++) and database would you choose? Why?"
Other topics included:

Multithreading: daemon threads, stopping threads, race conditions, locks, transient and volatile keywords, thread sleep, executors, schedulers, Runnable interface.
Exception Handling: final, finally, try-catch, throw vs. throws.

ii) OOPs Concepts

Key questions covered:

Explanation of inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, interfaces.
Differences between runtime vs. compile-time polymorphism.
Why Java doesn’t support multiple inheritance, with examples to illustrate potential conflicts.

iii) Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA)

Topics included:

Pseudocode for binary search, reversing a linked list, joining two numbers without a third variable.
Sorting algorithms: bubble sort, merge sort, insertion sort.
Advanced topics: frequency count, maximum subarray, binary search tree (BST), AVL tree, tower of Hanoi, red-black tree.

iv) Database

SQL-related tasks:

Writing queries to join two tables, find the 2nd largest/smallest salary, and employee queries based on salary and ratings.
Concepts: When to use WHEN vs. HAVING, running loops in SQL, triggers, query updates/deletions.
Theory:

Differences between RDBMS and DBMS, DDL, DML, ETL, ACID properties, indexing (clustered vs. primary).
Comparison of MongoDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, with scenarios for choosing each.

v) Projects

Detailed questions about the projects on my resume, focusing on technical implementation and challenges faced.

vi) Previous Work Experience

Discussions about my prior role, the tech stack used, and reasons for seeking a new opportunity.

vii) Git Commands

Basic Git commands were also part of this round.

3. Salary Negotiation and Role Discussion

In this round, the focus was on:

Your expected salary, role, and tech stack.
The project you would be assigned to.
Salary Insights:

Freshers: CTC: ₹25K (In-hand: ₹22,400).
6 Months’ Experience: ₹30–35K CTC, depending on interview performance. Exceptional performance could fetch ₹35K, while average results might lead to ₹25K.

4. Optional Round with the Company Owner

This optional round, if conducted, revolves around:

In-depth questions about the tech stack on your resume.
Your motivation for joining Coral Telecom and understanding of the organization.

Overall Experience

The overall interview experience was positive, with a medium difficulty level. The process tested a variety of skills, including technical expertise, problem-solving, and adaptability.
