experiences.title: Couchbase | UI/UX Role | Full Time | On-Campus | Interview Experience
experiences.full_content:
Couchbase Interview Experience for UI/UX Role

I recently had the opportunity to interview for a UI/UX role at Couchbase, a prominent database company. The recruitment process was conducted on-campus at my college, VITAP, where a significant number of students were invited to apply.

Application Process

The application process began when our campus recruitment team shared a link to apply for the position. Many students submitted their applications, and two days later, the company released the shortlist of candidates. It appeared that Couchbase primarily selected candidates based on their resumes, focusing on CGPA (with a preference for those above 9.0) and relevant project experience.

Shortlisted Candidates

In total, 120 candidates from four VIT campuses were shortlisted for interviews. From my college (VITAP), twelve students made the cut, including myself, for the UI/UX role.

Interview Structure

The interview process at Couchbase was structured into three main rounds conducted over a full day:

Technical Interview 1

Technical Interview 2

HR Round

Technical Interview 1

The first round was scheduled for 9:00 AM and lasted approximately 25-30 minutes. The interview focused on:

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Concepts: Questions were posed to assess my understanding of OOP principles.

Java Fundamentals: I was quizzed on my knowledge of Java and its features.

Data Structures: Questions included basic concepts and their applications.

Coding Challenge: I was tasked with finding the subarray with the maximum sum. The interviewer asked me to share my screen and code in an online IDE. I successfully completed this challenge.

After the first round, I awaited results until around 12:00 PM. Out of the twelve candidates, only five, including myself, advanced to the next round.

Technical Interview 2

My second round commenced at 3:00 PM. The focus shifted to my specific role as a UI/UX candidate, and the interview included:

Project Discussion: I was asked about my web development projects, with particular emphasis on technologies like React.js.

Practical Coding Task: I was provided with an online IDE and tasked with creating a basic React application that included a search bar connected to a REST API. Unfortunately, I encountered errors while coding. I communicated this to the interviewer, who was understanding and supportive.

The interviewer then presented me with a Java question involving a list of points, asking me to determine if they were collinear. I carefully handled edge cases and successfully coded the solution.

At the end of this round, I was instructed to wait for the HR call.

HR Round

By 6:00 PM, I had yet to receive any communication regarding my progression. Out of the five candidates from the second round, only two were selected for the HR interview. I was among the shortlisted candidates.

However, while other candidates received notifications regarding their status, I did not. Eventually, I learned that another candidate from my college received the HR call. Concerned, I reached out to my college's Career Development Center for clarification. They informed me that my profile had been rejected, and only one student from our group of twelve was selected for the HR round.

Conclusion

Overall, my interview experience with Couchbase was a valuable learning opportunity, despite the outcome. The process was well-structured and provided insights into both technical skills and role-specific knowledge. For anyone looking to interview with Couchbase, I recommend focusing on your projects and being prepared for both theoretical and practical assessments.

experiences.title: Cvent Interview Experience for SRE Role - On campus
experiences.full_content:
A month ago, Cvent visited our campus for a placement drive. There was an initial shortlisting of students based on GPA and other criteria. The entire process consisted of five rounds, completed in a single day.

Round 1: Technical Aptitude

This round included around 30 MCQ-based questions on an online platform, covering core CS subjects such as DSA, OS, DBMS, and others.

Round 2: Coding Round

Number of problems: 1

Duration: 30 minutes

The test was conducted on an online proctored platform, with 3-4 sets of problems randomly assigned. My problem was based on graphs. The task was to find the shortest path from city 1 to city N, starting from city 1. Each city was assigned a character. From city x, one could move to x+1, x-1, or any city with the same character in a single move.

My approach involved using a priority queue, similar to Dijkstra's algorithm. I initially inserted city 1 into the priority queue with a distance of 0. Then, I repeatedly popped the city with the minimum distance and added other reachable cities. I also implemented minor optimizations to prevent revisiting cities by marking distances. Though this may not be the most optimal approach, it passed all the given and hidden test cases (as confirmed during the interview).

Round 3: Technical Interview 1

In this round, I was asked to explain the code I wrote in the previous round, along with its time and space complexity. The interviewer confirmed that my code passed all the test cases. We also discussed my expertise, previous projects, and internships. Additionally, there were a few questions on machine learning and deep learning, though they didn't delve too deep (likely to test how I handle questions outside my expertise). There were also some basic questions about DevOps tools. My interview was quite relaxed, but some of my friends were asked separate DSA problems and core CS questions.

Round 4: Technical Interview 2

This was a more intense round, lasting about 1.5 hours. The interviewer asked detailed questions about my project from my first internship, focusing on aspects like data flow, packages used, and optimizations. We spent around 30 minutes on the project.

Next, I was asked questions from core CS subjects such as DSA, Computer Networks, OS, and OOPs. The questions were mostly basic to medium-level, covering a wide range of topics. Regarding DSA, he mainly asked about data structures like linked lists and their real-life applications. Some of my friends were also asked separate DSA problems.

Later, we discussed AWS and specific technologies such as EC2. I was asked why AWS is preferred over private servers, how to scale a web server, and more. There were also a few questions on DevOps tools, but these were not very deep, possibly due to time constraints.

Round 5: HR Round

This was a friendly and relaxed round. The HR representative was approachable, and we had a general discussion without any tricky questions.

Final Result: Cleared

experiences.title: D. E. Shaw Interview Experience | Systems FTE
experiences.full_content:
D.E. Shaw offered the highest on-campus CTC, making it a highly sought-after opportunity during placements. Like many others, I applied and embarked on a rigorous, theory-intensive interview process.

Round 1: Online Coding Assessment

The first round consisted of two sections:

Coding Questions:

Question 1: Medium difficulty – I solved this completely.
Question 2: Hard difficulty – I passed 13/15 test cases.

Core CS and Math MCQs:

17-20 multiple-choice questions were asked, focusing on core computer science concepts and math puzzles.
This section had a strict 20-minute time limit.
Out of 65 eligible students, 7 students were shortlisted for the next round, and I was fortunate to be one of them.

Round 2: Technical Interview

This round was held a week after the assessment and covered a wide range of core CS concepts. Key topics discussed during my interview included:

Introduction and Projects:

A brief introduction followed by a detailed discussion of my favorite project.

Core CS Concepts:

Multithreading vs. Multiprocessing
Thread Pooling
Process Scheduling Algorithms and Data Structure Choices
Process Synchronization and IPC Mechanisms
Profilers

Networking Fundamentals:

TCP vs. UDP
Working of UDB/GDB (Debuggers) and their underlying data structures
DNS, MAC and IP, Subnets, DHCP, ICMP, Packet Loss
What happens when you enter a URL? (Detailed explanation)
NAT and ARP

Programming and Concepts in C/C++:

Virtual Functions and Polymorphism (Runtime vs. Compile Time)
malloc vs. calloc
Inheritance vs. Composition
Inline Functions in C and C++
Thread Affinity
Crash Dump vs. Core Dump
Normalization

Resume-Based Questions:

Stock-market project: “What classes must be implemented in the Zerodha app?”
I answered most of these questions confidently and was advanced to the final technical round.

Round 3: Final Technical Round

This round involved an in-depth discussion about every concept and tool mentioned on my resume. The interviewers were well-versed in core CS concepts and keenly identified weaker areas in my knowledge.

Resume-Based Questions:

Detailed questioning about projects and strategies.
My approaches were countered, and I had to defend my choices.

Advanced Topics:

Thread Pooling and Thread Affinities (a known weak area for me).
Interrupts and System Calls.
User Mode vs. Kernel Mode, Mode Bit, and more.

Problem-Solving Task:

The final question involved designing a mechanism to handle machine failures in a distributed system:
Scenario: Machines A and B communicate with a server to perform tasks. If either fails, the other must take over from the failure point or start from the beginning.
My Solution: I proposed a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) mechanism where both machines log their transactions into a shared space before execution. I also suggested using a stack or bidirectional queue as the data structure for this mechanism.
The interviewers were satisfied with my solution, and the round concluded positively.

Verdict

I was offered a 6-month internship with a full-time role at a CTC of 56-58 LPA and a stipend of 2 LPM.

Key Takeaways

1. Core CS Knowledge:

Revise core computer science topics like networking, OS, data structures, and algorithms in extreme detail.
2. Resume Mastery:

Be prepared to defend and explain every concept/tool you mention on your resume.
3. Practical Problem-Solving:

Anticipate scenario-based questions and prepare solutions for system design problems.

Final Thoughts

The interview process at D.E. Shaw was intense but rewarding. It pushed me to deepen my understanding of core concepts and enhanced my problem-solving skills. For aspirants, focus on core CS topics, build strong projects, and stay confident. Best of luck!

experiences.title: D.E.Shaw Ascend Educare Program for women Experience
extracted_questions: What is the Ascend Educare Program?
experiences.full_content:
Hello everyone!

I am a pre-final year student at NIT Delhi. Although I'm not a professional writer, I’m writing to share my experience with the D.E. Shaw Ascend Educare Program.

What is the Ascend Educare Program?

D.E. Shaw is a global investment and technology development firm founded in 1998. The Ascend Educare Program is a six-month mentorship initiative for women in tech, launched in 2021. The main aim of this program is to engage women in the technical field and represent women’s participation in real-world intellectual projects. Through this program, students gain a better understanding of work culture and real-world projects at D.E. Shaw. Additionally, D.E. Shaw provides a stipend of approximately INR 50,000 for the entire duration of the program.

Eligibility Criteria

The Ascend Educare Program is only for women in engineering and is not open to male students. The eligibility requirements are as follows:

Second- and third-year female students of B.Tech/B.E. programs are eligible.
Third- and fourth-year students in a five-year dual degree program are eligible.
First-year students in a two-year M.Tech/MS/MCA program are eligible.
Second-year students in a three-year MCA program are also eligible.

Program Rounds

Round 1: Resume Shortlisting

This is an elimination round, where your resume plays a crucial role. If your resume is shortlisted, you advance to Round 2.

Round 2: HackerRank Online Test

This test was conducted on HackerRank with proctoring and consisted of two sections:

Section 1: Eight aptitude and computer fundamentals questions.

Section 2: Two coding questions, ranging from medium to hard difficulty. One of the questions in this section was very challenging, and only a few candidates could solve it. Students who managed to solve even half of this question were invited to the next round.

Round 3: Technical Interview

Most candidates were eliminated in the previous round, with only a few reaching the interview stage. This round lasted about 45 minutes. The interviewer asked for an introduction in the first five minutes, followed by two coding questions of medium to hard difficulty. Topics for these questions included linked lists and graphs.

My Experience

After being shortlisted for Round 2, I received an email about the online assessment. This round included two coding questions and eight multiple-choice questions based on computer fundamentals and aptitude. The overall test time was 90 minutes, and switching between questions was not allowed—each question had to be submitted before moving to the next. This round was challenging, with two coding questions of medium to hard difficulty.

After qualifying for this round, I received an invitation for a technical interview, which was conducted entirely online. The interview started with a brief introduction, and the interviewer asked two medium-difficulty coding questions. The entire interview lasted for 45 minutes.

Overall, my experience with the Ascend Educare mentorship program was positive. I hope sharing my experience will help others preparing for the program.

Thank you!

Question 2.1)

Problem Statement:

"Find the length of the longest substring that contains only vowels in a given string. Return both the substring and its length."

Example:

- Input: `"earthproblem"`

- Output: `('ea', 2)`

- Input: `"letsgosomewhere"`

- Output: `('e', 1)`

Python Code to Solve the Problem:

```python

def longest_vowel_substring(s):

vowels = set('aeiouAEIOU')

max_length = 0

current_length = 0

max_substring = ""

current_substring = ""

for char in s:

if char in vowels:

current_length += 1

current_substring += char

if current_length > max_length:

max_length = current_length

max_substring = current_substring

else:

current_length = 0

current_substring = ""

return max_substring, max_length

Example usage:

string1 = "earthproblem"

string2 = "letsgosomewhere"

print(longest_vowel_substring(string1))   Output: ('ea', 2)

print(longest_vowel_substring(string2))   Output: ('e', 1)

Explanation:

1. Vowel Set: We define a set of vowels (`aeiouAEIOU`) to check whether a character is a vowel.

2. Loop Through the String:

- We iterate over each character in the string.

- If the character is a vowel, we increase the `current_length` and add the character to `current_substring`.

- If the `current_length` exceeds `max_length`, we update `max_length` and set `max_substring` to `current_substring`.

3. Resetting:

- When a non-vowel character is encountered, we reset `current_length` and `current_substring` to zero and an empty string, respectively.

4. Result:

- The function returns a tuple containing the longest vowel substring and its length.

Possible Related Questions:

1. Find the Longest Substring Containing Only Consonants: Similar to the above problem, but you focus on consonants instead of vowels.

2. Find the Number of Substrings Containing All Vowels at Least Once: This would involve finding substrings that contain each vowel (`a, e, i, o, u`) at least once.

3. Count the Total Number of Vowel Substrings in a Given String: Instead of finding the longest one, count how many substrings in total consist only of vowels.

4. Find the Longest Substring Without Repeating Vowels: You could modify the problem to ensure that no vowel is repeated in the substring.

Each of these variations challenges you to think about string manipulation and efficient iteration over characters in Python.

Question 2.2)

The Correct Question:

"Write an SQL query to find the top 5 most sold products by summing up the sales details in the `sales` table and displaying the product name along with the total sales. Use an appropriate join between the `products` and `sales` tables."

Tables Structure:

1. `products` table:

- `product_id`: Unique identifier for each product.

- `product_name`: Name of the product.

2. `sales` table:

- `product_id`: References the `product_id` in the `products` table.

- `sales_amount`: Amount of sales for the product.

SQL Query to Solve the Problem:

SELECT p.product_name, SUM(s.sales_amount) AS total_sales

FROM products p

JOIN sales s ON p.product_id = s.product_id

GROUP BY p.product_name

ORDER BY total_sales DESC

LIMIT 5;

Explanation:

1. Join: The `JOIN` clause is used to combine rows from the `products` and `sales` tables based on the `product_id`. This allows you to access both the product name and the sales data.

2. Aggregation: The `SUM(s.sales_amount)` function calculates the total sales for each product.

3. Grouping: The `GROUP BY p.product_name` groups the results by each product name, so the sum is calculated per product.

4. Sorting: The `ORDER BY total_sales DESC` sorts the results in descending order based on total sales, so the product with the highest sales comes first.

5. Limiting: The `LIMIT 5` ensures that only the top 5 products are returned.

This query will give you the names of the top 5 most sold products along with their total sales amounts.

1) Find the total sum of each participant's marks and display their name and total marks.

You can loop through the participants list, calculate the sum of the marks for each participant, and then display their name along with the total marks.

2) Find the maximum marks obtained by a participant and display their name.

You can keep track of the maximum marks while iterating through the list and display the participant's name who obtained the maximum marks.

3) Possible Question:

A common follow-up could be to find the average marks of each participant and display their name and average marks.

Here's the Python code to accomplish all of these tasks:

python

Copy code

participants = [

{"name": "John", "marks": {"math": 40, "physics": 50, "chemistry": 70}},

{"name": "Alice", "marks": {"math": 55, "physics": 65, "chemistry": 75}},

{"name": "Bob", "marks": {"math": 60, "physics": 70, "chemistry": 80}}

]

1) Calculate the total marks for each participant and display their name and total marks

for participant in participants:

name = participant["name"]

total_marks = sum(participant["marks"].values())

print(f"{name} has total marks: {total_marks}")

2) Find the participant with the maximum marks and display their name

max_marks = 0

top_scorer = ""

for participant in participants:

total_marks = sum(participant["marks"].values())

if total_marks > max_marks:

max_marks = total_marks

top_scorer = participant["name"]

print(f"The participant with the maximum marks is {top_scorer} with {max_marks} marks.")

3) Calculate the average marks for each participant and display their name and average marks

for participant in participants:

name = participant["name"]

total_marks = sum(participant["marks"].values())

num_subjects = len(participant["marks"])

average_marks = total_marks / num_subjects

print(f"{name} has an average of {average_marks:.2f} marks.")

Explanation:

Total Marks Calculation:

For each participant, the total marks are calculated using sum(participant["marks"].values()) which adds up the values in the marks dictionary.

The result is displayed using the participant's name.

Maximum Marks Calculation:

We maintain a variable max_marks to track the highest marks found so far.

As we iterate through each participant, if their total marks exceed max_marks, we update max_marks and set top_scorer to the current participant's name.

Average Marks Calculation

The average is calculated by dividing the total marks by the number of subjects.

The result is displayed with the participant's name.

experiences.title: Datazip Inc Interview Experience  | On-Campus
experiences.full_content:
As a final-year student, I recently participated in the university recruitment process for a DevOps role at Datazip Inc. Known for its innovative, no-code, scalable data platform, Datazip offers exciting opportunities for aspiring DevOps professionals. The recruitment process was rigorous, involving an initial online DevOps assignment, an online test, and a technical interview. Although I didn’t make it to the cultural round, the experience was invaluable and offered numerous learning opportunities. Here’s a detailed account of my journey.

URL- https://datazip.io/Datazip Inc. Datazip Inc. is a cutting-edge company in the DevOps domain, providing a powerful platform that simplifies data ingestion, storage, transformation, and visualization. Their focus on enabling fast, data-driven decision-making makes them a highly sought-after employer for those passionate about DevOps and data engineering.

Recruitment Process

a) Initial Online DevOps Assignment: The recruitment process kicked off with an online DevOps assignment. This assignment tested our hands-on knowledge of DevOps tools and methodologies. We were tasked with setting up CI/CD pipelines, automating infrastructure deployment, and working with Docker and Kubernetes. It was a challenging assignment that required practical skills and a solid understanding of DevOps practices.

b) Online Test: Candidates who completed the assignment were shortlisted for an online test. The test was comprehensive, covering topics such as Linux commands, scripting, cloud computing, containerization, and system design. The questions were designed to assess both theoretical knowledge and the ability to apply that knowledge to real-world scenarios. It was a demanding test that required both speed and accuracy.

c) Technical Interview: Having cleared the online test, I advanced to the technical interview round. This round was intense and focused heavily on my understanding of DevOps principles, tools, and technologies. The interviewers asked detailed questions about my previous projects, especially those related to DevOps, and presented real-world scenarios to gauge my problem-solving abilities. Despite the pressure, I managed to navigate through most of the questions, demonstrating my technical expertise and logical thinking.

The Outcome

Unfortunately, I did not progress to the cultural round. While the technical interview went well, I wasn’t selected to move forward in the process. Although it was disappointing not to advance, I took this experience as a learning opportunity.

Reflections and Learning

The recruitment process at Datazip Inc. was a valuable experience that pushed me to hone my DevOps skills and think critically under pressure. The process also highlighted areas where I could improve, particularly in aligning my technical knowledge with real-world applications and better preparing for future interviews.

While I didn’t make it to the final stage, the experience has motivated me to continue improving and learning. For anyone preparing for a similar role, I recommend a strong focus on both technical skills and real-world applications, as well as staying resilient and open to learning from every experience.

Conclusion Although my journey with Datazip Inc. ended earlier than I had hoped, the experience was a significant step in my professional growth. It reinforced the importance of technical expertise, problem-solving skills, and the ability to adapt quickly to new challenges. I’m grateful for the opportunity and look forward to applying what I’ve learned in future opportunities.

experiences.title: D.E Shaw Interview Experience for Technology Developer Intern 2025
experiences.full_content:
ROUND 1: Online Assessment

This round consisted of three coding questions based on topics such as binary search, dynamic programming, and prefix sums. The eligibility criteria were a CGPA of 7+ for the IT branch and 8+ for the ECE branch. Over 300 students were eligible for the online assessment.
The difficulty level of the questions ranged from medium to hard, and a total of 16 students were shortlisted for the next round.

ROUND 2: Technical Interview - 1

This round was conducted in both online and offline modes. I participated in an online interview via HackerRank CodePair.
There were two interviewers, and the round began with my introduction and a discussion about my projects. My project focused on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Deep Learning, and I was asked several related questions.
Next, I was presented with a coding question: N Repeating Substring.  https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/find-given-string-can-represented-substring-iterating-substring-n-times/
I was expected to explain my approach, code the solution, and pass the given test cases. I successfully coded the optimal solution, which satisfied the interviewer.
Following that, the first interviewer asked questions about Operating Systems (OS), covering topics such as virtual memory, paging, segmentation, physical vs. virtual memory, and fragmentation. The discussion delved into various related topics, requiring a comprehensive understanding of OS concepts.
The second interviewer focused on Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), asking questions about method overloading, method overriding, the static keyword, and runtime polymorphism.
The interview concluded positively, with the interviewers expressing satisfaction with my answers. They then invited me to ask questions, and I inquired about the work culture and technology stacks used by interns.
Out of 16 candidates, 10 students were shortlisted for the next round.

ROUND 3: Technical Interview - 2

This round was conducted offline for all students, with two interviewers on the panel.
The round began with my introduction, followed by questions about my project and related technologies.
I was then asked a Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) question: to create a custom class with the following specifications:You are given a canvas of size n x m, initially filled with 0. You can perform the following operations:draw(r, c): Draw a shape (represented by an alphabet from 'A' to 'Z') on cell (r, c). If multiple shapes are drawn on a cell, the most recent shape is displayed.
delete(r, c): Delete the most recent shape from cell (r, c). If multiple shapes are present, the most recent shape is removed, revealing the next most recent. If no shapes exist, 0 is displayed.
move(r1, c1, r2, c2): Move the shape from cell (r1, c1) to (r2, c2), following the same rules for multiple shapes. The question was initially vague, and I had to ask several follow-up questions to clarify the requirements. My first solution processed each operation in O(N) time. However, when asked to optimize it, I proposed a solution using a hashmap and queue that achieved O(logN) time per operation, which satisfied the interviewer.

The second interviewer then asked about OOP concepts, specifically regarding constructors and the private access specifier. I was challenged to create an object of a class with only a private constructor. I suggested various approaches using the static keyword and getter/setter methods, but the interviewer was not satisfied.
Another DSA question followed: Given two numbers represented as linked lists of the same length, I was tasked with adding the numbers under the following constraints:Reversing the linked list is not allowed.
Modifying the linked list is not allowed.
Extra space is not allowed.
Recursion is not allowed. This problem was non-trivial since I had to add the numbers in reverse order. Initially, I proposed an O(N^2) solution, but the interviewer requested optimization. After spending 10-15 minutes thinking through the problem and explaining my thought process, I presented an optimized approach that seemed to satisfy the interviewer.

The interview concluded with the opportunity for me to ask questions.
Results were announced on the same day, with three students receiving offers.

experiences.title: D.E. Shaw & Group Interview Experience | Systems Engineer Intern
experiences.full_content:
Recently, D.E. Shaw & Group visited our campus to recruit students for the Systems Engineer Intern role. Here’s a detailed account of my experience throughout the entire process.

Round 1: Online Assessment

The recruitment process kicked off with an online assessment conducted immediately after the pre-placement talk. All eligible students participated in this assessment in a lab, proctored by representatives from D.E. Shaw and our university faculty.

The assessment consisted of:

One DSA question based on Dynamic Programming.
Three MCQ sections: Technical MCQ, Aptitude, and Systems-based MCQ.
The total duration of the assessment was 45 minutes, with specific durations allocated to each section. Out of 109 students, only 17 were shortlisted, and I was fortunate to be among them.

Round 2: Technical Interview I

The next phase was the first technical interview. Two panels, each comprising two members from D.E. Shaw, interviewed the shortlisted students. The interview questions primarily focused on:

Projects listed on our resumes.
In-depth OOP and database concepts (such as normalization and query performance).
I managed to answer most of the questions confidently. At the end of this round, only four students, including myself, were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 3: Technical Interview II

The second technical interview involved the other panel that did not interview us initially. This round featured questions on:

Data Structures and Algorithms (specifically BFS and DFS).
Backend development(since I had projects revolving that field in my resume)
Brain teasers designed to test our problem-solving abilities.
Unfortunately, I struggled with a few questions in this round, which affected my chances. Out of the four candidates, only two were selected, and I wasn’t one of them.

Although I didn't make it to the final selection, the experience was immensely valuable. It provided me with insights into the recruitment process of a prestigious firm like D.E. Shaw & Group and highlighted areas where I can improve for future opportunities.

I hope this detailed account of my experience helps you understand the rigorous recruitment process and prepares you better for similar opportunities.

experiences.title: Deliveroo | Interview Experience | Intern + Fulltime | On-Campus ( 2024 )
experiences.full_content:
During the placement season, Deliveroo visited our campus for the role of Software Engineer. They visited the campus around the last week of July, 2024. The company had a four-step recruitment process after the Pre-Placement Talk. The eligibility criteria to apply was a minimum of 8.0 CGPA with no active backlogs, only for B.Tech. CSE and IT.

Round 1: Online Assesment

The Online Assesment was conducted on the Hackerrank platform and had 3 coding questions as follows:

Question 1) Given an array denoting the release times for different products.Also given another array denoting the alternate times in which the respective products can be released.We had to return the minimum time in which all the products can be released.Constraint:The products need to be released in the order as in the first array, for example in array1, if product1 has a release time of 5 and product2 has a release time of 6 then no matter what their alternate release times are, product1 needs to be released before product2. I was able to solve it completely using greedy approach.

Question 2) Given Strings of URLs as an array called "Requests", we had to print the output for each Request.The output had to be as follows:

1) if the request had arrived less than 5 units of time ago then the output should be "error"

2)else the output should be "resolved"

the index was the time of arrival of the request. I was able to solve it completely using HashMaps.

Question 3) Given an array of edges of a graph, we had to find the sum of weights of the Spanning Tree of the graph which had the Maximum edge weight of that spanning tree - Minimum edge weight of the same spanning tree as minimum among all the spanning trees.I was able to solve it partially using Prim's Algorithm + Dynamic Programming, A more  optimal approach would have been Kruskal's Algorithm(using Disjoint Set Union) + Dynamic Programming.

The time provided for this assesment was 90 minutes.

After the online assesment 60 people were shortlisted for the interview process.

Round 2: Technical Interview 1

This round was held in offline 1:1 mode. The interviewer was very chill and we started with our introduction and jumped straight to the first DSA Question.

Question 1) The question was same as https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/sum-numbers-formed-root-leaf-paths/

I first gave him a brute force approach using DFS + Strings and then optimized it using DFS + a static global variable and he was satisfied with the solution.Then he moved on to the next question.

Question 2) The question was same as https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/find-smallest-range-containing-elements-from-k-lists/

I took around 5 to 7 minutes just to understand the question but the interviewer was very helpful in explaining the test cases.I gave him a K-pointer approach which was the brute force approach for this problem and it was correct.So the interviewer pointed to a certain section of the code and asked me if I can optimize it, and he also gave some hints and fortunately I was able to catch those hints and presented him an optimal solution using K-pointers and priority queue and he was satisfied.

Though the round format was 2 questions to be solved in 60 minutes but I solved the two questions in around 30 minutes itself, so he gave me a 3rd question.

Question 3) Given a grid filled with 0's and 1's and I had to return the area of the smallest rectangle(in terms of area), that includes all the ones in that grid.

Within 1 minute I came up with a solution andexplained him what we can do to solve it.He was very impressed and asked me if I had solved this question before.(The solution is : find the minimum and maximum row indices that contain 1 and the total rows in the rectangle would be max - min + 1, similarly for columns find the minimum and maximum column indices that contain 1 and the total columns in the rectangle would be max - min + 1, the result would be the product of these 2).

So I solved all the questions in around 40 minutes.So we had time left so I was curious about the interviewer and the company so I asked him a few questions like, How was it for him when he was a fresher?, How different is his work in Deliveroo from  his previous company etc.

Since this was an offline round, we had to write the pseudocode on paper.Some of the candidates had online interview and they had to do type the same thing on a notepad.

Tips: be very vocal about your approach and before typing / writing anything, first communicate it with the interviewer and then proceed.

Around 29 people were shortlisted for Round 3.

Round 3: Technical Interview 2

This round was called the System Thinking Round, where my interviewer was a highly experienced individual with over 16 years in the industry, having worked for various big tech companies. We first introduced ourselves and then quickly moved to the problem statement. I was given a lengthy paragraph and had to extract the functionalities to create: 1) a Normalised Database Schema, and 2) a High-Level Design.

The problem statement was centered around a plot-selling platform with functionalities like selling plots, signing license agreements, advertising plots in various newspapers, etc. The interviewer was very supportive; I was a bit confused about some of the terminologies, so I asked many clarifying questions to fully understand the problem. He was patient and explained everything in clear, unambiguous terms.

The round was conducted online, and the interviewer provided a link to Drawback.io, where I created the schema. I designed around 17-18 tables, each with their respective attributes highlighting the primary keys, foreign keys etc. Afterward, I was asked to explain the relationships between the tables (e.g., one-to-many, many-to-one, etc.). I answered correctly for most relationships, except one, which the interviewer gently guided me through by saying, "Are you sure? Think again." That prompt helped me come up with the correct answer.

Next, I was asked to write a medium-level query based on my schema, which I successfully did using subqueries. As time was running short, the interviewer asked me to pick any functionality from the application and outline its High-Level Design, detailing the flow from frontend to backend—how data would be extracted from API requests and stored in the database using specific queries, etc. I chose the license agreement signing functionality and presented the high-level design. Initially, there was some confusion regarding my frontend functionality, but I clarified how I envisioned the frontend working and how that would impact the backend operations. I also included additional considerations like load balancing and multiple servers for fault tolerance and less load on a single server.

At the end, the interviewer’s reaction was neutral, leaving me a bit unsure if he was satisfied or not. We concluded the interview with a few questions from my side.

Tips: Use technical jargon confidently, and don't hesitate to ask questions or clarify doubts about the problem statement instead of making assumptions and heading in the wrong direction.

Around 14 people were shortlisted for the 4th round.

Round 4: Behavioural Interview Round

This was more of an HR + technical round as my interviewer had a technical background as well. She was very friendly, and we started with introductions before jumping straight into the questions. She asked me basic HR questions, such as whether I had worked on any ambiguous projects in the past, how I resolved conflicts with teammates, what my biggest weakness is, and how I am working on it. I answered these questions based on my past experience and referenced the projects I had worked on to support my responses.

In one of my projects, I had used a database locking mechanism to handle concurrency issues, specifically pessimistic locking. She was curious about why I didn't use optimistic locking or any other technology and what other options I could have considered. She also asked what improvements I would implement if I had to build the project from scratch again. I explained why I implemented the technologies I had chosen, the trade-offs involved, and what I learned from the project.

experiences.title: Delloite Us Interview Experience

How would you act in a particular scenario type of questions were asked to me.

I had the opportunity to participate in the hiring process conducted by Deloitte at SASTRA Deemed University, Tanjore for the roles of Analyst and Cyber Security. Here’s a detailed account of my journey through the selection process.

Eligibility Criteria

CGPA: Minimum of 6.0
Backlogs: No active backlogs

Round 1: Online Assessment

The first round was an online assessment that tested:

Aptitude: Quantitative, Verbal, and Non-Verbal Reasoning
Coding: Two basic-level coding problems
Out of approximately 700 participants, 127 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 2: Online Interview

The interview was conducted on the company’s official platform, where candidates were assigned specific time slots. However, I faced a two-hour wait due to scheduling delays. Additionally, connectivity issues on the interviewer’s end caused a couple of interruptions before the session stabilized.

Introduction

The interview started with a self-introduction, where I discussed my educational background and experiences at SASTRA Deemed University.

Technical Questions

The interviewer then asked about my mini-project:

What was your project?
I explained the project’s objectives, tools, technologies, challenges, and my contributions.
What would you like to change in the project?
What technical difficulties did you face?
How could you improve it?

Behavioral Questions

The interviewer assessed my teamwork and problem-solving skills with the following questions:

What difficulties have you faced working in a team, and how did you resolve them?
What does success mean to you?
Have you ever faced failure? How did you overcome it?
How do you approach achieving a goal?
Why should we not hire you?
Do you plan to pursue a master’s degree?
Are you comfortable reporting to someone younger than you?

Coding Question

The final part of the technical round included a coding problem using the inbuilt compiler:
Problem: Minimum steps to climb a staircase (similar to problems on GeeksforGeeks or Leetcode).

Final Thoughts

Participating in the hiring process conducted by Deloitte was an insightful and rewarding experience. Despite the delays and technical issues, the process was comprehensive, allowing me to showcase my technical skills and problem-solving abilities.

This experience highlighted the importance of preparation, adaptability, and confidence in handling real-world challenges. It was a privilege to represent SASTRA Deemed University and take part in this opportunity.

experiences.title: Deloitte India | Interview Experience | ADMM Analyst | Full-Time | 2025 Batch On Campus
experiences.full_content:
Deloitte India came for 6-7 practice areas in our college.

First round (Online) was common to all but we were asked to select 2 preferences while filling the form.

First Round was Online Assessment which included 50 questions to be solved in 60 mins. There were 3 sections with respective session time limit.

Quants & Logical - 20 que in 25 min
Verbal - 10 que in 10 min
Computer fundamentals - 20 que in 25 min
(Further rounds were said to be offline but due to some reasons, it was taken online)

Deloitte then released practice area wise shortlisted students for further process. My 1st preference was ADMM and I got that for further process. Now on, it will be ADMM specific.

Second Round was Group Discussion(GD) in which 34 students were divided into 3 cohorts. The topic for all was same and related to EV automobile company whose sales is quite good but post sales experience and lack of digitalization is worst, due to which, there is lack of satisfaction to customers and now sales can degrade; propose solution for the same. We discussed it for 15 mins and then we were asked 1 ques on each. A s per GD, 19 people received mail for 3rd round.

In 3rd round, interview was taken by a Director at Deloitte, the interview was quite chill. Topics on which my interview are as follows:

Introduce yourself, Your thoughts on Gen AI, What is Gen AI and its use cases in real life & industry, Projects, Internships, Hackathons, Have you ever worked on Gen AI ,3 Important factors to create an successful AI model, Data Cleaning & Have you ever worked on this?

Note: Interview was in a flow as the following questions asked by interviewer were mostly on what I answered to current questions. It was easy if you know what you have done and written in resume and you communicate it well with confidence and clarity. My interview went towards my participation in hackathons, projects (engineering curriculum ones and personal) and AI & Data Analysis as I showed my interest and respective internships.

Fourth Round : After few hours, we received a mail which had 16 names and were asked to join together in a meet and wait. Randomly, 3 people were taken in and interviewer was Partner at Deloitte. experiences.title: Deloitte India  Interview Experience | ADMM Analyst | Full Time
experiences.full_content:
In September, Deloitte India visited our campus for recruitment, offering 7 Analyst roles across various domains, including Marketing and Management, HRT, Oracle & SAP, and others. I applied for the ADMM Analyst (Application and Data Modernization and Migration) role.

Here’s a breakdown of my recruitment journey, which spanned over three days.

Day 1: Online Assessment

The first round was an online test with three sections, each containing 20 questions:

Quantitative Aptitude
Verbal Ability
Technical Section (Covered CS fundamentals like DBMS, OS, CN, Python, OOPS, and Pseudocode)

Difficulty Level:

Quants and Verbal: Easy
Technical: Easy to Medium
Verdict: CLEARED

We received the shortlist for the next round the evening before the interviews.

Day 2: Group Discussion, Panel Interview, and Partner Interview

1. Group Discussion (GD):

Shortlisted Candidates: 75 (for my role)
Process:Groups of 12 were formed, and each group joined a virtual meeting with a panelist.
We were given a topic, had 15 minutes to discuss, and then each participant got 1 minute to summarize their points.

Challenges:

The online format made the discussion phase chaotic, with only 4–5 members able to actively contribute. I was one of those unable to participate fully. However, the concluding phase leveled the playing field as the panelist judged each candidate on the uniqueness of their points and articulation during the summary.

Verdict: CLEARED
Results were announced within an hour.

2. Panel Interview:

Shortlisted Candidates: 41
Process:
My interview was postponed twice due to scheduling delays, resulting in a wait of about 3 hours. When it finally began, the interviewer focused on my resume, discussing:My projects
My internships
What I had learned from them

Questions:

Basic CS fundamentals (questions varied for each candidate).
Some candidates were asked to code, though my interview didn’t include coding.
Duration: 20 minutes
Verdict: CLEARED

3. Partner Interview:

Shortlisted Candidates: 24
Process:
Groups of 3 were invited to a meeting with one of Deloitte India’s partners. This was the most relaxed round and felt more like a casual conversation.

Discussion Points:

General Conversation: Experiences so far and life in the hostel.
Individual Introductions: Overview of resumes, hobbies, and interests.
Role Insights: The partner provided details about the ADMM Analyst role and a glimpse into a typical day at Deloitte.
The atmosphere was informal, and the discussion was enjoyable, making it a pleasant conclusion to the process.

Final Results

After a one-day gap, the final results were announced. Out of all the candidates, 21 Analysts were selected for the ADMM role, and I was thrilled to be one of them!

Tips for Future Aspirants

Know Your Resume: Be thorough with your projects, internships, and skills.
Master CS Fundamentals: Revise key concepts like DBMS, OS, CN, and OOPS.
Group Discussion: Focus on presenting unique points clearly and confidently, especially during the summary.
Stay Relaxed and Engaged: The Partner Interview is more about your personality than technical knowledge.
The recruitment process with Deloitte India was a great learning experience. For anyone preparing for a Deloitte interview, focus on your fundamentals, stay confident, and most importantly, enjoy the journey!

experiences.full_content:
I recently appeared for the HashedIn by Deloitte placement drive conducted at my college, and I’m thrilled to share that I was SELECTED!  I’m writing this post to walk you through  interview rounds, and share some tips that might help you in your journey.

Round 1: Online Assessment (90 mins)

This was an online test consisting of three coding questions of varying difficulty levels. While I don’t recall the exact problems, here’s a breakdown of the topics they covered:

Candies Allocation Problem  (Easy one using greedy Approach ).
A Binary String Problem to find the maximum no of ones after flipping all the digits within an continuous range (Medium To Tough Difficulty Level ).
A variant of the Problem Related to Next Greater element in an array (Medium Difficulty).
Each question carried points, and I managed to solve All three questions. Consistent Practice, especially from platforms like GFG and Leetcode, helped me perform well.

Round 2: Technical Interview 1 (45-50 min)

The interviewer was extremely friendly and supportive, which helped create a positive atmosphere. The session began with introductions and a brief discussion about my internship experience. Following this, I was given 3-4 DSA questions to solve, after which the interviewer asked a series of DBMS-related questions, including SQL queries.

The questions included:

Missing and Repeating element in an Array.
Find Pairs whose sum equal to an target sum.
Find Longest Palindromic Substring in an Array.
Merge K sorted Lists
I solved all four questions, starting with brute force approaches and optimizing them to better and optimal solutions. However, I got slightly stuck while optimizing the fourth problem.

After the coding section, the interviewer asked the following DBMS and Resume related questions:

Difference between Unique and Primary key
Difference Between Where and Having Clause.
What Are SQL Commands
SQL query related questions which involved some basic DDL queries.
what are React Hooks (Since I mentioned React in my resume).
How does JWT Authentication Works.

I was able to answer all the questions, and the interviewer seemed satisfied with my responses.

Round 3: Technical Interview 2 (1 hr 10min)

This round began with my basic introduction, after which the interviewer asked me to explain one of my projects. I described an e-commerce application I built using Next.js. Since the project utilized a MongoDB database, the interviewer delved into a discussion about SQL vs. NoSQL databases. Following this, I was asked to write a query using both SQL and NoSQL.

Next, I was given a DSA problem based on the graph data structure:

Given a 2D matrix containing a source node, a target node, and some blocked nodes, find the longest path from the source to the target.

I solved this problem using DFS (Depth First Search).

Afterward, I was tasked with designing a database for a restaurant table booking application. This included:

Database design with proper schema.
Creating an ERD (Entity-Relationship Diagram).
Writing queries for all the requested features.
With the interviewer's guidance and my preparation in database design, I successfully completed this task.

Round 4: HR/Managerial Interview (20 min)

This was the final round, and it primarily consisted of common HR questions along with a few situation-based questions. Some of the key questions I was asked include:

From which place do I belong?
A brief introduction about my family.
What can I bring to HashedIn?
Why should they hire me?
What do I know about HashedIn?
In addition to these, I was presented with 2-3 situation-based questions, which I answered confidently.

Finally, the results were declared, and I was thrilled to be among the 7 students offered a position by HashedIn from my campus.

I would like to thank my mentors, peers, and seniors who guided me throughout my preparation journey. Their support and advice were invaluable. I am also grateful to the HashedIn by Deloitte team for providing such a wonderful opportunity and conducting the process so smoothly.

experiences.title: Deloitte Interview Experience for SDE
experiences.full_content:
I recently had the opportunity to interview with Deloitte for a Software Developer position, and I wanted to share my experience to help others who might be preparing for similar roles. The entire process took about two weeks and involved several stages, each focusing on different aspects of my technical and behavioral skills.

Application Process

I applied for the position through Deloitte’s career portal. A few days after submitting my resume, I received an email from a recruiter inviting me to schedule an initial phone screening. The recruiter also provided some details about the interview process and what to expect.

Round 1: Phone Screening

The first round was a phone screening with the recruiter. This was a fairly straightforward conversation where they asked about my background, experience, and interest in Deloitte. They also provided more details about the role and the team I would potentially be working with. There were no technical questions in this round, but they did ask about my availability and salary expectations.

Round 2: Technical Screening (Online Test)

The next stage was an online technical test. This was conducted on a platform like HackerRank or Codility and included a mix of coding challenges and multiple-choice questions. The test was divided into three sections:

Coding Problems: Two coding problems tested my problem-solving and algorithmic skills. One problem was medium difficulty, involving array manipulation, while the other was more challenging, requiring knowledge of dynamic programming.
Multiple-Choice Questions: This section focused on core computer science concepts, such as data structures, algorithms, databases, and a bit of system design. There were also questions about basic software engineering principles, like OOP, design patterns, and best practices in coding.
SQL Queries: A few questions required writing SQL queries to fetch and manipulate data from a given database schema. These were fairly straightforward but required a good understanding of SQL joins subqueries, and aggregate functions.
I was given 90 minutes to complete the test, and I found the time constraint reasonable but challenging, especially for the second coding problem.

Round 3: Technical Interview

After successfully passing the online test, I was invited to a technical interview with a senior developer from the team. This interview lasted about an hour and was conducted over video conferencing.

Coding: The interviewer started with a live coding session where I was asked to solve a problem using a shared coding environment. The problem was similar in difficulty to those in the online test, focusing on arrays and strings. The interviewer was looking for clean, efficient code and also tested my ability to explain my thought process as I coded.
System Design: Next, I was given a system design question where I had to design a simple application (e.g., a URL shortening service). The interviewer was interested in how I approached the problem, my understanding of scalability, and how I handled trade-offs in the design.
Two coding problems tested There were also questions about my previous projects, especially those related to technologies mentioned in my resume. We discussed my experience with specific programming languages, frameworks, and tools. The interviewer also asked me to explain the architecture of one of my recent projects and how I contributed to it.

Round 4: Behavioral Interview

The final round was a behavioral interview with the hiring manager. This interview was more focused on assessing cultural fit, communication skills, and how I would handle various situations in a team environment.

Situational Questions: I was asked several STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) questions about how I handled challenges in past projects, how I work under pressure, and how I deal with conflicts in a team setting.
Team Collaboration: The interviewer also wanted to know how I collaborate with cross-functional teams, especially in an Agile environment. They were particularly interested in my experience with Agile methodologies, such as Scrum or Kanban.
Motivation and Goals: Finally, the interviewer asked about my long-term career goals, why I wanted to join Deloitte, and how I saw myself growing within the company.

Offer and Conclusion

A few days after the behavioral interview, I received a call from the recruiter with an offer. They provided a detailed compensation package and explained the benefits, as well as next steps. I was given some time to review the offer and ask any additional questions.

Overall, the interview process was thorough and well-structured. Deloitte was very professional throughout, and the interviewers were friendly, making the experience less stressful. I appreciated the focus on both technical and behavioral aspects, as it gave me a good sense of the company's values and work culture.

For anyone preparing for a similar role at Deloitte, I would recommend brushing up on your coding skills, especially in algorithms and system design, and being ready to discuss your past projects and experiences in detail. Good luck!

experiences.title: Deloitte Interview Experience| On-Campus Placement Drive 2024 (Product Engineering Analyst Role)
experiences.full_content:
Introduction

I recently participated in the Deloitte On-Campus Placement Drive for the Product Engineering Analyst role held in 2024. The offered package was 7.6 LPA, with a base salary of 6 LPA. Approximately 600 to 700 students applied for the position, and the entire process consisted of four intense rounds. Here’s a step-by-step account of my experience with the preparation, interview rounds, and key takeaways.

Interview Rounds Breakdown

Round 1: Online Assessment

Format: MCQs and two coding questions
Difficulty: Easy
Topics: Logical reasoning, aptitude, and DSA (basic array and string problems)
The coding problems were straightforward. I encountered one problem based on array manipulation and another on basic string processing. After the results, only 60 students were shortlisted from the initial pool of 600-700.

Round 2: Group Discussion

Topic: "AI Replaces Humans"
Duration: 30 minutes
Group Size: 10 participants
This round tested our communication, teamwork, and leadership skills. I ensured that I contributed meaningfully to the discussion while also listening to my teammates. After 15 minutes of group discussion, 38 candidates advanced to the next round.

Round 3: Technical Interview

This round focused heavily on the technical aspects of my resume and the skills I listed.

Key Questions:

Resume Walkthrough: I was asked to explain the key projects mentioned in my resume.
Project Discussion: I detailed a full-stack MERN project, specifically about how I handled student data management and the overall application flow.
API Explanation: The interviewer asked me to define an API and describe how I would integrate one into my project.
Coding Problem: I was tasked with identifying the next number in the sequence: 5, 10, 35, 75, 195, which required logical reasoning and pattern recognition.
Database Query: I was asked to write a join query in SQL to fetch data from multiple tables.
OOP Concept: I explained inheritance and its real-world applications in Java.
This round was a mix of project-related discussions, coding problems, and OOP concepts, lasting about 30 minutes.

Round 4: Behavioral Interview

The final round aimed to evaluate my soft skills and understand my personality.

Key Questions:

Self-Introduction: I provided a brief introduction about myself.
Academic Performance: The interviewer asked why there was a difference between my intermediate and B.Tech scores.
Skills Discussion: I was tested on my problem-solving skills with questions like:Find the first repeating character in a string.
Write a function to return character frequencies in a string, focusing on characters appearing more than twice.

Project Impact: I explained the real-world implications of my projects.
Unique Qualities: I was asked to list three qualities that set me apart.
Confidence Level: I was asked if I felt confident about being selected when I entered the interview.
Future Goals: I described where I see myself in five years.
Strengths and Weaknesses: The interviewer inquired about my strengths and areas I need to improve.
At the end, the interviewer advised me to avoid using AI-generated resumes and to focus on keeping my resume authentic and concise.

Final Verdict

After a challenging and rewarding interview process, I’m thrilled to share that I was selected for the Product Engineering Analyst role at Deloitte. The Deloitte interview process combines technical and behavioral assessments, making it crucial to be well-rounded in both areas for success.

experiences.title: Deloitte USI Interview Experience for Analyst |  On-Campus 2024
experiences.full_content:
Deloitte USI visited our campus in August 2024 to recruit for the role of Analyst. The process was thorough and well-structured, testing candidates on multiple skills. Here's an overview of the placement drive, my experience, and tips for aspiring candidates.

Eligibility Criteria

No active backlogs.
Aggregate score of 60% or more.

Placement Drive Overview

The placement process consisted of three stages:

Resume Shortlisting
Online Assessment
Technical + HR Interview

1. Resume Shortlisting

Most applicants cleared this round, making it an inclusive start to the process.

2. Online Assessment (90 Minutes)

Platform: HirePro

The assessment was divided into timed sections, each testing a specific skill area. On average, about one minute was allotted per question, with 20 minutes set aside for two coding problems.

Assessment Breakdown

Analytical Ability
Quantitative Ability
Verbal Ability
Computer Science Fundamentals: Topics included OS, DBMS, Cloud Computing, SQL, and pseudocode.
Coding Questions: Two problems (1 Easy, 1 Medium).
I managed to solve almost all MCQs and both coding questions, finishing with 6-7 minutes to spare.

Results: Out of around 300 applicants, 49 students were shortlisted. I was fortunate to be one of them.

Tip: Speed and accuracy are critical. Proper time management can make a significant difference in this round.

3. Technical + HR Interview (30–50 Minutes)

The final stage of the process began with a Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) by the Deloitte USI team. Eleven senior employees shared insights into the company's culture, values, and opportunities.

Tip: Take notes during the PPT. Referencing the company’s values or panel introductions during your interview shows genuine interest.

After a short break, one-on-one interviews began. Each interviewer's approach varied—some focused on HR questions, while others emphasized technical skills. My interview focused entirely on technical topics.

My Interview Experience

Interviewer Background: A Full Stack Java Developer with eight years of experience at Deloitte USI.
Interview Flow:Project Discussion: Detailed conversation about my projects and their implementations.
Scenario-Based Question: I was asked to suggest improvements for an autonomous parking system.
SQL: Basic queries were tested.
DSA Question: A LeetCode easy-level problem on searching and sorting, where I provided both brute force and optimized solutions.

At the end of the interview, I asked the interviewer about his role and responsibilities, which he explained in detail. The session lasted about 50 minutes.

Tip: Be confident, know your projects thoroughly, and don’t lie on your resume.

Results: The results were announced the same day, and I was selected!

Key Takeaways and Tips

Be Confident: Nervousness can cloud your performance, so try to stay composed.
Know Your Projects: Expect in-depth questions and potentially coding challenges based on your project work.
Honesty is Crucial: Misrepresentation on your resume can lead to disqualification.
Research the Test Platform: Interviewers often have access to your test performance analytics.
Practice Puzzles: Some candidates were asked puzzles or situational questions—resources like GFG can be helpful.
Presence of Mind: Always stay alert and think logically during the process.

Conclusion

The Deloitte USI placement drive was a demanding yet rewarding experience. It provided insights into my technical abilities and taught me the importance of preparation, confidence, and adaptability. While the day was long and tiring, the joy of being selected made it all worth it!

I hope my experience helps you navigate your interviews more efficiently. Best of luck!

experiences.title: Derrick Jones Management Interview Experience
experiences.full_content:
The interview began with a warm greeting from the interview panel, which included a Senior Manager and the Branch Manager. They started with an overview of the company’s vision for the New Zealand Study Visa Department and shared insights into the role of a Team Leader.

1. Introduction and Background

Question: "Can you briefly introduce yourself and describe your background in visa processes and team management?"

Response: I introduced myself, highlighting my strong background in immigration services and my expertise in handling New Zealand visa processes. I mentioned my progression from SOP Writer to Team Leader at Derrick Jones Management, emphasizing my experience in overseeing visa applications, conducting client interviews, and leading a team to meet regulatory standards.

2. Role-Specific Skills and Responsibilities

Question: "Can you describe a challenging case you've managed and how you resolved it?"

Response: I explained a complex visa application I handled, where the client had an incomplete financial document. I detailed how I worked closely with the client to secure the necessary documentation, coordinated with the financial team, and ensured timely submission. This experience demonstrated my problem-solving skills and commitment to regulatory compliance.

3. Team Leadership and Management

Question: "How do you ensure your team meets quality standards in documentation and client handling?"

Response: I shared my strategy of conducting regular file reviews and providing targeted training sessions to keep the team updated on compliance regulations. I described my approach to setting clear goals for team members, holding daily briefings, and fostering open communication, ensuring everyone understands quality expectations.

4. Client Relations and Interview Preparation

Question: "Client satisfaction is crucial. How do you handle escalated client concerns?"

Response: I explained that my approach involves listening actively to client concerns, addressing issues promptly, and providing clear communication throughout the visa process. I also shared an example of a time when I helped a nervous client prepare for their interview, which led to a positive outcome.

5. Process Optimization and Compliance Knowledge

Question: "What steps do you take to keep up with changes in immigration policies?"

Response: I mentioned my commitment to continuous learning and attending cross-training sessions, especially regarding regulatory changes in New Zealand immigration laws. I also highlighted how I implemented streamlined processes for the team to improve efficiency, such as optimizing file review stages and adopting a systematic checklist for document submissions.

6. Future Vision and Growth

Question: "Where do you see yourself contributing most to our company’s goals in the next few years?"

Response: I shared my aspiration to build a more streamlined visa application process, foster strong client relationships, and contribute to Derrick Jones Management’s reputation as a trusted provider in study visa applications. I expressed my desire to take on additional responsibilities, including cross-department collaboration to enhance overall client support.

7. Closing Remarks

The interviewers were impressed by my dedication to process optimization and client satisfaction. They concluded by asking if I had any questions, and I inquired about upcoming projects for the New Zealand Study Visa Department. This question led to a positive discussion on growth opportunities, which seemed to leave a favorable impression.

Technical Round 2

My Experience of Round 1 - Technical Interview at Deutsche Bank

Deutsche Bank is rapidly growing in the Technology, Development, and Innovation (TDI) sector, positioning itself as a prominent FinTech company. Here’s a detailed account of my experience during the first round of the technical interview.

This experience not only tested my technical skills but also highlighted the importance of thoroughly knowing my resume and being prepared to discuss and demonstrate my knowledge in a clear and concise manner.

Duration: Approximately 1 Hour

A. Coding Task: We were required to write actual code on a sheet of paper, not just pseudocode or algorithms.

B. Interview Questions: The questions were primarily based on my introduction and the content of my resume. Please note that they did not expect any prior knowledge of banking or finance.

Interview Questions Breakdown:

Introduce Yourself
Coding Question 1: Implement a sorting method of your choice.
Discussion: Which is the best sorting method?
Comparison: Difference between Merge Sort and Quick Sort.
SQL Query: Write a query to display the element with the highest ID from a sorted (in ascending order) database.
SQL Query: Write a query to display the element with the highest ID from an unsorted database.
Conceptual Question: Explain the difference between DBMS and RDBMS.
Real-Life Examples: Provide real-life examples of a LinkedList and a Stack.
Coding Question 2: Write code to insert elements (stored in an array) into a Binary Search Tree (BST).
Time Complexity: Discuss the time complexity of both pieces of code written.
Project Discussion: Provide detailed explanations about the projects listed on your resume.
Framework Knowledge: Explain more about the JSP framework mentioned in your resume.
OOP Concepts: Explain method overriding and overloading.
Access Specifiers: List and explain different access specifiers.
Constructors: Explain what a constructor is and how it works during inheritance.
Questions for the Interviewer: Tip: Always ask at least one question to show your interest and engagement.

Follow-Up Rounds:

After the technical interview, there were two more rounds: the ProFit (Professional Fitness) round and the final HR round.

I was selected, and I will be posting details for the next round soon.
